items.title: Where are the campaigns for 2027? By Tonnie Iredia
items.description: As soon as a new president was sworn into office in Nigeria on May 29, 2023, politicians began to campaign for the 2027 elections that were 4 years away establishing clearly that they are in power for personal gains only. Political analysts shouted in vain that the continuation of electioneering at the end of one set of elections was unhealthy for a developing nation such as Nigeria which had suffered largely from stultified growth. No good hospitals anywhere; the few health related structures had no drugs or other medical necessities. Our schools had no teachers and teaching facilities – learning under trees was still rampant. The rural communities were worse off as many supposed school buildings in such locations were grossly dilapidated. How can Nigeria grow with its office holders ceaselessly politicking? The rest of us could not stop the insane posture which was almost completely interspersed by defections of opposition politicians into the ruling party in search of part of the national cake. Political materialism has thus continued unabated presenting a political scenario never seen before in such a large scale in Nigeria. At a point, the Independent National Electoral Commission INEC was forced to condemn the celebrated premature campaigns. Quoting Section 94(1) of the Electoral Act, INEC warned that political campaigns could only commence 150 days before the next election adding that it had not at the time issued a timetable for the next election cycle. In the absence of specific legal sanctions for premature campaigns, INEC called on the National Assembly to criminalize the trend. Nothing was done because those who can push for sanctions are quite often the main culprits thereby encouraging relentless ‘jumping of the gun’ campaigns. Interestingly, the same irrational politicians who have damaged governance and the economy are nowhere to be found now that signals authorising open campaigns to start have been given by INEC. What we have said so far suggests that our politicians have little respect for law. In earnest, campaign efforts are always feeble with the few politicians engaged in them restricting themselves not to vigorous explanations of their policies and plans but merely drawing attention to perceived weaknesses of their opponents. In another clime, the electorate would at this point be expecting politicians to come forward to account for their stewardship. In Nigeria in particular, political office holders and their parties have a lot to account for. Apart from explaining what they could not do and what they did poorly, they have an obligation to explain the behaviour of changing the mandate of the people. How for example does a person elected under party A explain his defection to party B when political defections are not legally encouraged in Nigeria? It is only legislators that are allowed to defect but even at that, defection is tolerated only under specific circumstances. A defection is deemed to be illegal if the party involved does not have a crisis that is national in nature. In other words, it is not enough to have crisis or disagreement at local or state levels, it must be big enough to affect the structure of the national body before a legislator can defect to another party. In the case of the executive branch, no one expected a governor with a gamut of infrastructural challenges to waste time thinking of moving from one party to another. But in Nigeria our governors now do so to the shock of many. If I voted for a person to become the governor of my state under party A and he defects to party B which I did not vote for, he has an obligation to explain his action now; otherwise, I will not in another election vote for such an unstable person. Nigerian voters are therefore expected to task all those who defected to a party that the voters did not originally vote for because by so doing, the defectors had breached the democratic precept. Indeed, such defector-governors had taken the votes of one party to another in a country where votes by law belong to a political party and not the candidate that was sponsored. In another part of the world, the system would not allow anyone to appropriate the votes of others. But in Nigeria where everything can be experimented upon, the poor voter ought to at this point of campaigns for another set of elections insist on a proper explanation for why his vote was misdirected the last time to a party he deliberately shunned during the casting of ballots. It would therefore appear that the demand for accountability by defector-governors is the only option available to a voter in a country enmeshed in technical justice. In addition, campaigns should focus on substantive issues rather than frivolities. We have had enough of who is clueless or not. What we need now is what each person intends to do if elected and more especially how he intends to do them. Many people are not bothered about the popular point of who FCT Minister Nyesom Wike wants to support, we are also not anxious about whether the APC governors are happy or sad about the emergence of the Rainbow coalition. Even the contentious issue of fuel subsidy is being wrongly handled. It is true that Nigerians are currently living under hard conditions following the removal of subsidy. It is also an inconvertible fact that in the past when the subsidy policy existed, life in the country was also precarious. It is therefore unwise to support the removal or return of subsidy without an explanation of how each party’s position can improve the welfare of the common man. Today, there is no subsidy and all we hear is a sermon of patience – sweet grammar of light at the end of the tunnel while we are seeing flashes of light in some parts of the tunnel, economic jargons of micro and macro as well as plenty of funds now reportedly in the hands of governors while the poor are starving. One opposition party is telling us about the return of subsidy as if we are incapable of remembering the evils of fuel scarcity. The ADC candidate was in office as Vice President years back when the government of the day was virtually overwhelmed by the cartel that allegedly stole our oil. At this point of campaigns therefore, we ought to evolve a new posture where the issue at stake should not be the return or removal of subsidy but the management strategy to be applied to each position in the interest of the average citizen. Again, campaigns cannot be premised on visits to a handful of traditional rulers for endorsements because those visits in all honesty constitute blackmail. If a traditional ruler receives a team well, he is labelled the friend of the team and the enemy of its opponents; if so, why push royalty and the acclaimed father of all to a compromised corner? Instead, target the masses of the people whose votes matter more and campaign on the issues bothering them. Above all, campaign teams must be civil and they too must be given a fair chance to make its point, so that at the end of the day, voters are able to get well informed through political education that enables them to vote wisely. On a general note, efforts must be made during the campaigns to condemn violence by asking parties involved in it to give account. In the last few months some politicians especially members of the ruling party have been variously accused of intimidating others by sending party thugs to destabilize rallies by rival political parties. Locations where such attacks happen should send signals to all political parties that they have resolved not to vote for the visible aggressors in their domain. The point to be made is that violence cannot be the easiest way to know the better of two candidates. Best practices recommend political debates organized by the media. The Nigerian media should come forward to take charge of the subject with impartiality. No one should be excluded and the ruling party should not exclude itself because of the old belief that it is the one everyone else is targeting for attacks. The forum must be devoid of personal attacks as it is an educational platform to inform all about who can best govern society. As a result, common issues such as acute insecurity should be made the subject that everyone is to address. No one should be allowed to change campaigns from information and education purposes to entertainment with music and dancing where nothing meaningful is said. Furthermore, intemperate language must not be allowed and efforts should be made to isolate everybody’s standpoint as a basis for identifying what each party stands for. The post Where are the campaigns for 2027? By Tonnie Iredia appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Progress at UNGA
items.description: ALTHOUGH no breakthrough was achieved at the UN General Assembly, there has been some progress where finding a negotiated solution to the US war on Iran is concerned. For example, both the American and Iranian delegations held talks mediated by Qatar, while the Iranian president told Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif that Tehran was still committed to the Islamabad MoU. Moreover, other reports indicate that both the US and Iran are looking for an off-ramp, with Tehran offering to open the Strait of Hormuz for marine traffic if Washington ends its blockade of Iran. The key question is: who will blink first in this battle of wits, as neither side will want to appear weak? Now it is up to both sides — as well as the states mediating this conflict — to take forward the progress made in New York. As the US, along with Israel, initiated this aggression, it should take the first step and offer confidence-building measures to Iran in order to de-escalate the situation and come to a long-term settlement. Though White House officials have said Iran is ‘desperate’ for a deal, the fact is that high fuel prices are also hurting the Trump administration at home. An unpopular war coupled with high inflation is not likely to have a positive effect on the Republicans’ chances going into November’s midterm elections. In a meeting on the UNGA sidelines, Mr Trump’s Gulf allies reportedly asked him for a post-midterm strategy regarding Iran. Perhaps something can come out of the interactions at the UN. However, the talks must not be a ruse to open Hormuz and to merely suspend hostilities and stabilise oil prices until the US midterms. There are some indications that the Trump administration may be considering kinetic action after the elections. It would mean a disastrous new confrontation in the Middle East. Hopefully, wiser counsel will prevail in Washington. The way forward seems simple. The US must approach Iran with sincerity, and the talks must not be a smokescreen for further military action later. The blockade of Iran should be lifted and its funds released to enable a longer-term peace. Tehran, on its part, should commit to keeping Hormuz open in the interest of both its neighbours and the wider international community, while also refraining from targeting the Gulf states. Also, any new agreement should cover all fronts: Gaza, Lebanon and Yemen. Although these are separate conflicts, they are also interlinked as Iranian allies are involved in all of them fighting Israel, the US and Saudi Arabia. Hence, a peace treaty with Iran alone may not last unless there is also calm in other regional theatres, while there is a particular need to rein in Israel’s murderous attacks on regional states. Published in Dawn, September 27th, 2026

items.title: ATC acquits 7 more policemen ‘for lack of evidence’ in Naqeebullah Mehsud's murder case
items.description: KARACHI: After the acquittal of former Malir SSP Rao Anwar, an antiterrorism court on Saturday acquitted seven more policemen in a case over the killing of Naqeebullah Mehsud and three others in a staged encounter in January 2018. The then SHOs of Shah Latif Town and Sachal police, Amanullah Marwat and Shaikh Muhammad Shoaib alias Shooter; assistant sub-inspector (ASI) Gada Hussain; head constables Sadaqat Ali and Mohsin Abbasi; and constables Raja Shamim and Rana Riaz Ahmed were facing trial for allegedly killing Naseemullah, better known as Naqeebullah Mehsud, Mohammad Sabir, Nazar Jan and Mohammad Ishaq in an alleged staged encounter in January 2018. After examining the witnesses and hearing concluding arguments from both sides, the judge of ATC-VI exonerated the accused persons for lack of evidence. Prosecutor Anila Malik argued that the prosecution examined over 40 witnesses, including star witnesses and they linked the accused persons with the commission of offences and documentary evidence also corroborated their testimonies. Former SSP Rao Anwar was acquitted in the same case in 2023 She also contended that the prosecution established its case against all the accused persons beyond a shadow of reasonable doubt and pleaded for conviction. However, defence lawyer Farzana Mateen submitted that all accused persons facing trial were framed with mala fide intention and that out of 40, not a single witness directly implicated any of the accused in the case. She also maintained that there were glaring contradictions in the evidence of prosecution witnesses while two star witnesses about the abduction of Hazrat Ali and Muhammad Qasim did not associate the present accused persons in their statements recorded under Section 164 CrPC by a judicial magistrate and had also not identified these accused persons as the culprits during their evidence before the trial court. The defence lawyer further argued that there was no allegation of abduction of the deceased against the accused persons and the prosecution has also failed to prove their participation in the alleged encounter. She maintained that many accused persons, including a former senior superintendent of police, had already been exonerated by the trial court in the first round of litigation for want of evidence and she pleaded for acquittal of the present accused persons as well. Initially, the then SSP Malir Rao Anwar, along with his around two dozen subordinates, had been booked for allegedly murdering Naqeebullah and others in an alleged staged encounter in a Malir locality and dubbing them as militants. According to the prosecution, Naqeebullah was picked up with his two friends allegedly by eight to nine subordinates of Rao Anwar in civvies. Later, the other two detainees were set free while the whereabouts of Mehsud remained unknown and his mobile phone was also found powered off, as the former SSP allegedly kept him in wrongful detention. It further stated that on Jan 17, the captive’s relatives came to know through the media that Rao Anwar and his associates allegedly killed Mehsud and three others in a staged encounter in a Shah Latif Town area on Jan 13 and dubbed them as Taliban militants. The provincial police officer had constituted a three-member inquiry committee that found Rao Anwar and his associates involved in the case, it added. However, in January 2023, the trial court acquitted the former SSP and 17 members of his team by extending the benefit of doubt. As the state had opted not to impugn the acquittal order, a brother of Naqeeb had filed an appeal before the Sindh High Court against their acquittal. The present accused persons were absconders during the first trial, and after the exoneration of SSP and others, they had surrendered before the court to face the trial, and all of them were set free on bail in April this year. Published in Dawn, September 27th, 2026

items.title: Three booked for rape of Azeri woman in Lahore
items.description: LAHORE: Defence-C police on Saturday registered a case against three unidentified men on charges of subjecting an Azeri woman to gang rape. A 20-year-old Azeri woman was visiting Pakistan for business purposes and was residing in a house near Raiwind Road. She filed an application with the police stating that two women approached her for dinner. They went to a café where three men met them. She could identify the men and women by face. She said the men offered her and two other women to drive and they later took her to an unidentified flat. She said they consumed alcohol and she was also served some intoxicating material and fell unconscious. She said three men allegedly gang-raped her and later locked her in the flat till 2pm. She said the suspects came back and dropped her near Ghazi Interchange and fled the scene. She said the suspects also took away her mobile phone and other luggage. She demanded action against the suspects. Defence-C police registered a case against the three suspects and started the investigation. Published in Dawn, September 27th, 2026

items.title: Sharjeel promises action against men found riding pink scooters
items.description: MIRPURKHAS: Sindh Senior Minister Sharjeel Inam Memon has distributed free pink scooters among women in Mirpurkhas . Speaking at a ceremony held here on Saturday, he made it clear that the scooters were for women only and that action would be taken against any man seen using a pink scooter. He said Sindh was the only province in the country that is providing free e-scooters to women. “After providing training to women, e-scooters are being provided to those who pass the test,” he said, adding: “Our women are playing their full role in every field of life, and the Pakistan Peo­ples Party will continue such measures for the empowerment of women.” He said that pink taxis for women will also be launched soon. Mr Memon, who also holds the portfolios of information, transport and mass transit, said: “I do not know who the women coming here today are as the government is distributing pink scooters without discrimination and without distinction.” “The number of driving licences for women was previously very low; however, it is now increasing rapidly. I want to make it clear that this process of providing pink scooters to women is not going to stop. We want 50,000 women who obtain driving licences to be provided with EV scooters,” he said. He said empowering women was a reflection of the vision of former prime minister Benazir Bhutto, who launched Lady Health Workers, First Women Bank and other important projects for the empowerment of women. “Earlier, women in Sindh were not as independent as they are today. After the martyrdom of Shaheed Mohtarma Benazir Bhutto, President Asif Ali Zardari launched the Benazir Income Support Programme for deserving women, under which identity cards were made for many women, and consequently the number of voters also increased,” he said. “Today our women leaders, including Faryal Tal­pur, Dr Azra Fazal Pech­uho, Nafeesa Shah, Shazia Marri and others, are present in the assemblies on general seats. Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari and Presi­dent Zardari have issued special instructions for the empowerment of women,” he said. He said that Hari Cards were being issued for farmers and Labour Cards for workers. “Sindh is at the forefront in the fields of health and education, including Thar coal.” Provincial Minister for Culture Zulfiqar Ali Shah, Imdad Pitafi, Qasim Siraj Soomro, among others, were also present at the ceremony. Published in Dawn, September 27th, 2026

items.title: Tinubu’s re-election bid: Why Kaduna is more crucial than Lagos, Kano, Katsina, Rivers
items.description: By John Alechenu WHEN strategists, who have started working over time, especially inside Aso Rock, spread the big electoral map of Nigeria on the table to plot President Bola Tinubu’s path to a second term in 2027, Kaduna State will enjoy a pride of place. It is not Kano with the highest number of voters. It is not Lagos, the president’s political base. It is not even Katsina, home of the late President Muhammadu Buhari. Pundits argue that Kaduna is small enough to ignore at a casual glance, but big enough to ruin your entire calculation. The reason is simple. Kaduna is what some describe as mini-Nigeria because of its diversity. You have a largely Muslim Kaduna North and a predominantly Christian Kaduna South. You have Hausa-Fulani co-existing with Bajju, Atyap, Ham, Gwong and over 60 other groups. You have big urban problems and rural banditry in the same breath. It was capital of the old Northern Region and still carries what the late Second Republic politician, Dr Junaid Mohammed, described as “that old arrogance of power.” What happens in Kaduna reverberates across the North. For Tinubu, Kaduna matters for practical reasons. First, the votes. Kaduna sits in the North-West, the biggest voting bloc in the country. In 2023, over 93 million eligible voters were registered by the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, across the country. However, roughly 25 million voted. The zone had over 22.4 million registered voters and accounted for over 6.5 million votes. Kaduna alone had 4.3 million registered voters, the third largest in the zone after Kano and Katsina. But unlike Katsina where the All Progressives Congress, APC, can almost go to sleep and win, it has a real battle on its hands in Kaduna. Figures released by INEC after the 2023 presidential election showed Atiku Abubakar polled 554,360 votes, Tinubu came second with 399,293, while Peter Obi polled 294,494. The APC, however, won the governorship race. Back then, Atiku’s Peoples Democratic Party, PDP, held Southern Kaduna firmly and snatched parts of Kaduna Central. The Labour Party shocked many in Chikun, Kaduna North and parts of Igabi, riding on the anger of young and urban voters squeezed by the economy. Shared ownership That is Kaduna. No party can claim 100 percent ownership. You win it polling unit-by-polling unit, ward-by-ward. If you manage a convincing win there, you go into the general election with momentum. If you lose it, the headline alone demoralises your supporters in the rest of the North-West. A lot has changed since 2023. Only Tinubu has remained in his party, the APC. Atiku, Obi and others have since changed platforms and formed new alliances. From Zaria to Kafanchan, the conversation is different. In a tea joint, popularly called Mai Shayi, in Tudun Wada, the talk is about dollar rate. In a church in Sabon Tasha, it is about the cost of fertiliser. In Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria, lecturers debate tax reform. Dahiru Umar, a regular patron at the Mai Shayi joint, told Sunday Vanguard, “For those interested in business, the relative stability in the naira to dollar exchange rate will count for something. For most voters, the cost of everyday living remains a talking point.” Kaduna parades perhaps the most politically aware electorate in the North: Retired generals in Malali, former permanent secretaries, traders in Sheikh Abubakar Gumi market, farmers in Soba and Giwa. When the North is uneasy about a policy, you will probably hear it first in Kaduna. Opinion shaping institutions The state hosts institutions that shape opinion beyond its borders – the Jama’atu Nasril Islam, Council of Imams and Ulamas, CAN leadership, Emir of Zazzau, Agwatyap and other traditional rulers. Their statement in Kaduna travels to Sokoto, Maiduguri and Ilorin. For a president seeking re-election, controlling that conversation is gold. If Kaduna says things are improving, the North-West listens. A Zaria-based Islamic cleric, Sheikh Auwal Shariff, has been vocal about the economic impact of Tinubu’s fuel subsidy removal. He was invited and quizzed by security officials over his constant criticisms. In one of his sermons aired on social media, Shariff said, “Tinubu and Buhari are like Pharaoh and Haman. “There is no difference between them. If not for Tinubu’s lack of regard for Nigerians, how can you announce the removal of subsidy in your inaugural speech?” APC’s grip since 2025 Since the PDP lost power in 2015, Kaduna has remained in APC’s grip, but never as a monolithic APC state. Within the party, you still have the legacy CPC bloc that followed Buhari, the old ACN crowd, PDP defectors with their own structures, and the new youth base that joined during Tinubu’s campaign. El-Rufai, who governed the state on APC’s platform until 2023, championed the Muslim-Muslim ticket campaign, first in Kaduna before doing the same at the national level. Some of his actions and inactions while in office alienated him from sections of the state, especially the South. Although he championed and later co-opted other APC governors, especially from the predominantly Muslim northern states, he has since fallen out with the government he helped install. His successor, Governor Uba Sani has tried to break away from what many, particularly in the southern part, see as El-Rufai’s divisive politics. Sani has appointed Christians and ethnic minorities into his cabinet, visited communities that were once no-go areas, and toned down the ‘us-versus-them’ rhetoric. It has not solved all problems, but tension is lower than in 2023. For the Villa, Uba Sani is considered a strategic asset. If he stabilises Kaduna, Tinubu can point to the state as a laboratory for national unity under his Renewed Hope Agenda. If Kaduna slides back into killings in Kajuru, Kauru and Zangon Kataf, the opposition will use it as evidence that nothing has changed. Whatever anyone feels about him, El-Rufai was central to Tinubu’s victory in the North-West in 2023. He was vocal, mobilised, and convinced many sceptics in the core North that a southern candidate was the best bet. His fallout with the Presidency after the ministerial screening left a wound that may take a while to heal. He still commands loyalty among a section of the APC in Kaduna North, Kaduna South, parts of Igabi and among young urban voters who liked his blunt, reformist style. The Presidency knows writing off that bloc completely will affect turnout in city centres. Managing El-Rufai’s influence That is why there have been quiet moves to manage the situation – emissaries, private meetings, softening of public attacks. It is not really about El-Rufai the person. It is about thousands of canvassers and influencers who believe in him. For almost five years, Kaduna was synonymous with bad news. Kidnappings on the Kaduna-Abuja highway, bandits emptying villages in Birnin Gwari, communal clashes in Kajuru, train attack, farmers abandoning farms, transporters doubling fares. In the last one year, there has been relative improvement. The Kaduna-Abuja road is safer than it was, though people still travel with fear. Farming has resumed in some local governments. The Abuja-Kaduna train service is back and fully booked most days. Soldiers have remained in Birnin Gwari forests, and the state government is combining force with dialogue. If that improvement holds till 2027, Tinubu will have something concrete to campaign with in Kaduna. He can go to Rigachikun and say, “your road is open”. He can go to Birnin Gwari and say, “you are back to your farms”. Real question after security But security alone will not be enough. In Kakuri, Sabon Gari Zaria and Kafanchan market, the question is simple: How much is rice, fuel, school fees? Since subsidy removal, life has been hard. Federal allocations have gone up, but prices have also gone up. What people feel in their pockets will determine how they vote. Unfinished business of Muslim-Muslim ticket There is also the unfinished business of the Muslim-Muslim ticket. It cost APC votes in Southern Kaduna in 2023. The wound is largely healed. However, appointments, projects and the governor’s peace moves in Jema’a, Kaura, Zangon Kataf and Sanga are being watched in the Villa. If APC can raise its figures in Southern Kaduna in 2027, even by 15 percent, it becomes a powerful story of inclusion. At the end of the day, politics is about numbers and narratives. Kano will give numbers. Rivers will give drama and resources. Katsina will give Buhari’s legacy. But Kaduna gives legitimacy. A convincing win in Kaduna allows Tinubu to claim he has united a complex state and, by extension, a complex Nigeria. That is why every local government election in Kaduna, every ministerial visit, every kilometre of the Abuja-Kaduna-Kano road, every posting to the Defence Industries Corporation or the refinery matters. A Southern Kaduna indigene, Mr Luka Binniyat, said the importance of the state cannot be over-emphasised. He said, “Kaduna is important. Mr President and those around him know this and they are taking steps to ensure he wins come 2027. “For the first time in a very long time, a large percentage of the people of this state feel seen. “Appointments and distribution of projects have taken into account our diversity.” Another resident, Umar Farouk, however, said the president may be “living in a fool’s paradise” to assume all was well in terms of his chances in 2027. He said, “I don’t see President Tinubu having problems in Kaduna South. He will however struggle in the predominantly Muslim North because of the general feeling that their expectations for voting for a Muslim-Muslim ticket have not been met.” Dr Joseph Anuga, senior lecturer at the Department of Political Science, University of Jos, told Sunday Vanguard on telephone that a lot will be on the table in 2027. He said, “Not only Kaduna, the whole country should be of interest to every serious contender. Every vote can make or mar a candidate. In this clime, people vote for varied reasons. “Like we experienced in 2023, some will vote to prove which ethnicity or religion is dominant, others will vote for the system to remain, while others will vote for change based on what they consider today’s economic realities. “What should be of interest to all is a transparent process where voters will, to a large degree, believe that their votes count and that the outcome reflects the views of the majority.” Minister of Works, Mr David Umahi who is the Deputy Director General of the APC 2027 Presidential Campaign has told all who care to listen that Tinubu’s works – especially road projects – will speak at the polls. Speaking during one of several visits to the Kaduna section of the project, Umahi said: “The Abuja-Kaduna-Kano Road project is very dear to Mr. President. “The people of Kaduna State are happy and will definitely show their appreciation with their votes.” The road to 2027 does not bypass Kaduna. It runs right through its middle – from Rigachikun to Rigasa, from Zaria to Kwoi, from Giwa to Kafanchan. The post Tinubu’s re-election bid: Why Kaduna is more crucial than Lagos, Kano, Katsina, Rivers appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: SMOKERS’ CORNER: THE AGE OF POLITICAL ABSURDITY
items.description: More than ever, modern political leaders across the globe are issuing statements that defy logic, science and history. Yet, instead of facing ridicule, these figures are frequently met with applause from their supporters. Last week, when Polish foreign minister Radosaw Sikorski claimed that Poland could swiftly defeat Russia in a direct conflict, political commentators across the United States and Europe met his remarks with mild mockery. However, within Poland, social media exploded with enthusiastic endorsement. Rather than facing critical pushback, Sikorski’s exaggerated claim was embraced as gospel by supporters. This perfectly illustrates how readily absurd political rhetoric is now absorbed. In a 2019 interview, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, while discussing India’s air strikes against Pakistan, explained that he advised military officials to launch the attack despite heavy rain and cloud cover. He ‘reasoned’ that clouds would block Pakistani radars. Even though radars operate via radio waves rather than visual sight, his supporters championed the assertion as an example of “military genius.” Modi’s historical claims are often even more surreal, such as his declaration that the birth of Karna in the ancient epic Mahabharata proves that test-tube baby technology was invented in ancient India. In a live 2021 television QnA, former Pakistani Prime Minister Imran Khan attributed rising sexual violence to women wearing “vulgar” clothes. He argued that “men are not robots” and that “if a woman wears very few clothes, it will have an impact on the men.” When he was criticised by women activists, his supporters (including many women) rallied around him, asserting that his critics were trying to undermine “traditional cultural values.” In an age of algorithmic outrage, identity politics and collapsing trust in institutions, the most outrageous claims can become expressions of loyalty and powerful instruments of persuasion Following the Taliban’s takeover of Kabul in 2021, Khan praised the event, declaring that the Afghan people had “broken the shackles of slavery.” The statement ignored the ensuing human rights crises while framing a complex geopolitical takeover as a glorious anti-imperialist victory. Many of his supporters applauded his ‘bold’ statement. During the global Covid vaccination drive in 2021, then-Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro warned citizens that taking the Pfizer vaccine could cause people to turn into alligators and make women grow beards. His core evangelical support base accepted this without hesitation. In the US, Donald Trump remains a master of uttering similar hogwash. During his first presidency, he dismissed global warming threats by claiming that rising sea levels would simply create “more oceanfront properties.” He reduced a complex ecological crisis to a real estate opportunity while ignoring basic coastal geography. His supporters praised his insightfulness. Illustration by Abro These are just a handful of examples highlighting a shift in modern political discourse. This move from facing ridicule for spouting outright nonsense to this nonsense enjoying widespread applause is the result of some drastic changes in media ecosystems, societal psychology and the nature of modern political power. The primary engine driving the acceptance of absurd statements is what the American academic Dan Kahan calls “identity-protective cognition.” According to Kahan, when political identity becomes tightly tied to a group, individuals process information not to evaluate its objective truth but to protect their status within the group. Accepting an absurd claim made by the group’s leader confirms an individual’s loyalty to the group, whereas rejecting the claim means aligning with political opponents. Research led by the American professor of psychology and neural science Jay Van Bavel suggests that political loyalty in this regard acts as a “cognitive filter.” It overrides basic critical thinking and yields psychological rewards that reinforce one’s sense of belonging to a group, even when a leader’s claim contradicts reality. Historically, mainstream media often acted as gatekeepers. A ridiculous statement was processed through editorial standards, highlighted for its absurdity and derided on public platforms. Western media used to take apart various leaders for this — for instance, leaders such as Uganda’s dictator Idi Amin, who was reduced to being a joker, and Libya’s Muammar Gaddafi. Now the same West is struggling to comprehend mouthy far-right leaders in its own backyard. In Pakistan, Pir Pagara was often treated as a jester for making outlandish political predictions. Cartoonists often showed him with a parrot. Altaf Hussain was another politician who was regularly satirised and ridiculed, even though, to his followers he was a ‘visionary’. Till the 1990s, such characters were exceptions. Today, they are a norm. The rise of algorithmic platforms has gradually dismantled the role of gatekeepers. Various studies show that repeated exposure to a statement increases its perceived truthfulness, regardless of how implausible it sounds. Social media algorithms prioritise outrageous content because it drives engagement, causing absurd claims to be repeated millions of times in digital echo chambers. Studies by psychologists Gordon Pennycook and David Rand on misinformation show that repetition lowers a reader’s analytical guard, transitioning statements from sounding ridiculous to familiar and, eventually, to plausible and true. There are also studies that suggest that politicians, especially contemporary populists, do not utter absurdities by accident. They use them strategically. In their Rand Corporation paper on propaganda techniques, researchers Christopher Paul and Miriam Matthews coined the term “firehose of falsehood” to describe this “strategic disorientation.” The goal of flooding public space with continuous and blatantly absurd claims is not necessarily to convince everyone that a lie is true. It is used to exhaust the public’s capacity for critical thought. When politicians regularly spout absurdities, fact-checkers become overwhelmed. Academics at the global research network Evidence in Governance and Politics found that politicians, such as Trump, who aggressively dismiss corrections as ‘fake news’ retain public support and attention by sowing doubt about the mainstream media and fact-checkers themselves. Mouthy populist leaders are still roundly satirised, though. But when they routinely cross into surreal territory, satire loses its power. German-American political theorist Hannah Arendt wrote in The Origins of Totalitarianism that the ideal subjects of totalitarian rule are people for whom the distinction between fact and fiction no longer exists. When public trust in actual experts and state institutions collapses, expert consensus is no longer seen as a benchmark for truth. Instead, expertise is reframed as an establishment conspiracy. In this environment, an absurd statement from an ‘anti-establishment’ politician is perceived not as ignorance but as ‘bold defiance’ against a ‘corrupt’ system. The shift from ridiculing absurd political statements to believing them marks a transition from fact-based politics to identity-based politics. When an absurd claim is made, it serves as a flag planted by a leader in the ground. Followers do not process it through a filter asking if it is logically true. Instead, they spend more energy in contemplating which side they belong to if they accept or reject the claim. Until the dynamics and incentives of social media algorithms change and trust in shared institutions is restored, political absurdity will continue to erode as a punchline. Instead, it will solidify as a rather dangerous instrument of persuasion. Published in Dawn, EOS, September 27th, 2026

items.title: The 7th bid of Atiku – Fani-Kayode
items.description: By Femi Fani-Kayode In 1993, he contested the Social Democratic Party (SDP) presidential primaries and lost to MKO Abiola. In 2007, he contested as the Action Congress (AC) presidential candidate in the general elections and finished third behind Umaru Yar’Adua and Muhammadu Buhari. In 2011, he lost the PDP presidential primaries to incumbent Goodluck Jonathan. In 2015, he lost the APC presidential primaries to Muhammadu Buhari. In 2019, he was the PDP presidential candidate and lost the election to Buhari. In 2023, he was the PDP presidential candidate and lost the election to Bola Tinubu. 7th bid He is now on his 7th bid. There are only six documented cases of individuals who have contested the presidency of their country seven times or more. They are: 1) Pascual Racuyal of the Philippines who contested 11 times 2) Nicolás Zúñiga y Miranda of Mexico who contested 10 times 3) Harold Stassen of the United States of America who contested nine times 4) Jack Fellure of the United States of America who contested nine times 5) Lyndon LaRouche of the United States of America who contested eight times And finally… 6) Abdoulaye Wade of Senegal who contested seven times. Every single one of them failed to ever win the presidency of their nations except Wade who won on the 5th and 6th attempts and lost on the 7th. Atiku has failed in all of his six attempts over the last 33 years and he is now on his 7th. Stop and think about that. In a country of 230 million people, one man has been trying to be President for 33 years, has failed each time, and is now attempting it again for the 7th time. Again, consider the fact that the same man has been a member of seven political parties since he joined politics in 1991 and four political parties (one of which is the PDP which he left and rejoined twice) since 1999. Political wanderer Given this, it is fair to say that he is a political wanderer. Unlike leaders elsewhere, to Atiku, the party is nothing but a vehicle of power that exists for him and he does not exist for the party. It is of course his right to keep trying but this could also be legitimately regarded as an obsession. Nothing is more indicative of that obsession than his attempt to mobilise the governors of the PDP to move against his leader, President Olusegun Obasanjo, a man who had nominated him as his running mate for the second time, topple him as the party’s presidential candidate and take his place as the flag bearer in 2003. This was not only a case of ingratitude but also treachery and especially so because Obasanjo had trusted him to raise all the finances that were needed for that second run. Atiku allegedly raised the money through private donors and then tried to browbeat the President so that he would not be reelected. Two interventions saved Obasanjo. Firstly, the God factor, which was the most important, and, secondly, a stupendously wealthy businessman from Kano (who I shall not name) who made virtually all the money that was needed available for both the delegates at the convention and the election itself. That is how Atiku’s rebellion and ‘Absalom’ agenda was thwarted and crushed. Yet despite that Obasanjo refused to drop him mid-stream as his running mate and he was elected as Vice President on the same ticket of the man that he had sought to humiliate and destroy. Atiku is no Wade It was after the second term began after the 2003 election that the real war between the two camps began and I am proud to say that yours truly and others like Nasir El-Rufai, Nuhu Ribadu, Akin Osuntokun, Abiye Sekibo, Frank Nweke, Uba Sani, Adamu Bello, Julius Ihonvbere and many others that were either working in the Presidency or were Ministers together with others like Peter Odili of Rivers State, Umaru Yar’Adua of Katsina State, Ahmad Makarfi of Kaduna State and a number of other governors took the battle to the gates of the Vice President and gave him hell over the next four years. By the time it was all over, we had put him in his place and proved to him that treachery and rebellion are as the sin of witchcraft and never pay. His political career has not been the same since as he stumbled from one failed bid to the other leaving a legacy of division and destruction in his path. Some may argue that if Abdoulaye Wade of Senegal could eventually win after five attempts Atiku may do so after seven but the truth is that Atiku is no Abdoulaye Wade. He does not have the latter’s sincerity of purpose, courage, sense of loyalty, humility, discipline and patriotism. Outside of that, unlike Wade, Atiku Abubakar is more of a pragmatic businessman who is more interested in rebellion and treachery than a statesman who puts the interest of the nation before his own. Unlike Atiku, Wade would always endeavour to do the right thing by others, especially in the case of those who stood by him. Unlike Atiku, he appreciated the importance of loyalty, he did not covet the position of his leaders, he understood the power and dynamics of patience and he was not one to act desperately. Unlike Atiku, he NEVER tried to undermine, destroy, humiliate, discredit or topple his benefactors and neither did he attempt to dishonour standing agreements or deny others the presidency whenever it was their turn. Wade played politics within the rules and norms: he did not attempt to subvert or violate them to his own advantage. Atiku, on the other hand, revels in subversion and believes that Nigeria was established for his benefit alone. This is a man that has consistently opposed and fought against the idea of power shift to the South ever since he left office in 2007. He enunciated that notion and willingly espoused that grave and grievous injustice. He challenged Goodluck Jonathan in 2011, stayed with the coalition that removed him from power in 2015, took the PDP ticket from Nyesom Wike in 2022, ran against Bola Tinubu and Peter Obi in 2023 and is doing so again in 2027. Contempt for the South What remains striking is that he has done this even in cycles when power shift to the South was the prevailing argument from much of the political class, including many Northern leaders who backed it in the name of rotation, fairness and equity. Clearly, he has contempt for Southern aspirations. That is his mindset though he masks it well. Simply put, he has a sectional outlook and not a national one and for this reason God will not allow him to achieve his ambition. Outside of that, you cannot repay good with evil and escape it before the Lord. Atiku will learn this the hard way and so will those that stand with him. Is it any wonder that this time around he has employed the services of a controversial lobbyist to help him in return for a massive dollar fee? In the history of our country, we have never witnessed a presidential candidate employ foreign publicity firms to openly run down, threaten, slander and disparage the very Nigerians he wants to lead simply because he is so desperate to be President. Yet he will fail and, more importantly,, if the necessary evidence is adduced, he will be made to face the law for alleged corruption when he was Vice President. The most obvious allegation concerns the Mambilla Power Plant case but there are other allegations bordering on the Siemens case, the Halliburton case, the INTELS case, the William J. Jefferson U.S. Congressman case (for which the Congressman went to jail), the Leno Adesanya power plant case (which is reported to have been re-opened) and other serious allegations of corruption and offshore payments involving millions of dollars which, though yet to be proven, have left many unanswered questions. To be fair, none of these cases have, at least so far, resulted in a Nigerian trial or conviction but all have left a paper trail in the files of foreign regulators and many unanswered questions at home. Yet it didn’t stop there. Atiku’s worst crime was not the allegation of financial impropriety but his relentless determination to undermine and destabilise the government that he was elected to serve and to utterly destroy his principal whom he obviously hated with what the Bible described as “a perfect hatred”. Atiku betrayed Obasanjo to such a point that I, as Minister of Aviation at the time, was constrained to demand that he should be thrown out of Cabinet meetings on two separate occasions during full sessions of Cabinet. I did this during the course of the meeting and in the presence of every single Cabinet member and when I did so there was pindrop silence in the Cabinet chambers. The first time, Obasanjo saved him from the humiliation and appealed to me and the other Ministers to allow him to stay whilst he sat there looking daggers at me and clearly in a state of shock. The second time, which was a few weeks later, I made another demand in our Cabinet meeting under ‘other matters’ that if he did not get up and leave the chamber as a consequence of his betrayals and treachery against our President, then we the Ministers would walk out and leave him to conduct the Federal Executive Council meeting alone with the President. Obasanjo again appealed to us to allow him to stay but compelled him to apologise to the entire Cabinet there and then for his treachery and outrageous behaviour all motivated by the fact that he wanted to topple the President and take his place. Atiku apologised there and then to the entire Cabinet and consequently was allowed to stay at the Federal Executive Council meeting but he NEVER attended another Cabinet meeting after that. This episode proves how over-ambitious he was as Vice President and how he coveted the seat of the man that brought him out of obscurity in Adamawa State and made him his Vice President. He repaid Obasanjo’s good with evil just as he later repaid Tinubu’s, Buhari’s and the old PDP’s good with evil in later years. Today he is so desperate to win the presidential election that he has not only destroyed his old party, the PDP, by splitting it into two but he also did the same to the ADC, his new one, by breaking it in two and driving the Obi/Kwankwaso faction out to join a new party called the NDC. Anytime he does not get his way or his ambition to become the flag bearer of whichever party he is in is threatened, the party must be broken. In the case of PDP, he single-handedly killed what was once Nigeria’s dominant party and finally buried it in 2019. That is his political legacy: Chaos and destruction. Subsidy Worse still, as presidential candidate of the ADC, he has said he will restore fuel subsidy just to get votes knowing that in the process of implementing this disastrous policy he will utterly destroy Nigeria and cause us to lose all the economic gains we have made in the last three years. Let him be aware that there is nothing worse than attempting to destroy the future of your people just because you want to be President. Again let him be reminded that to pay a foreign PR company led by a controversial character who uses his wife’s surname rather than his father’s, $1.2 million to denigrate, undermine, demonise, vilify, malign and destroy your President in the international media just because you covet his seat is unacceptable. History is against you Waziri. No person in the world has ever tried to be President of his country seven times or more and has won except for Abdoulaye Wade and, like I said, you are no Wade and neither do you share his gravitas nor have his grit. Statistically and historically, you have little chance of winning on your seventh attempt or of ever becoming President. It appears that the Living God has placed a divine injunction on your ambition. This will be proved in January 2027 when you will be defeated by your old friend and arch-nemesis and be compelled to go back to Dubai and retire in peace. I come in peace, Waziri, and I wish you well. •Chief Femi Fani-Kayode is a former Minister of Culture and Tourism, a former Minister of Aviation, Nigeria’s Ambassador-Designate to South Africa, Lesotho and Estawani, the Sadaukin Shinkafi, the Wakilin Doka Potiskum, the Otunba of Joga Orile, the Aare Ajagunla of Otun Ekiti and a Legal Practitioner Waziri Atiku Abubakar, the former Vice President of Nigeria, has attempted to become President of our nation in no less than six times and his latest attempt is the 7th. In 2011, he lost the PDP presidential primaries to incumbent Goodluck Jonathan. In 2015, he lost the APC presidential primaries to Muhammadu Buhari. They are: 1) Pascual Racuyal of the Philippines who contested 11 times 2) Nicolás Zúñiga y Miranda of Mexico who contested 10 times 3) Harold Stassen of the United States of America who contested nine times 4) Jack Fellure of the United States of America who contested nine times 5) Lyndon LaRouche of the United States of America who contested eight times And finally… 6) Abdoulaye Wade of Senegal who contested seven times. Every single one of them failed to ever win the presidency of their nations except Wade who won on the 5th and 6th attempts and lost on the 7th. Atiku has failed in all of his six attempts over the last 33 years and he is now on his 7th. Stop and think about that. In a country of 230 million people, one man has been trying to be President for 33 years, has failed each time, and is now attempting it again for the 7th time. Again, consider the fact that the same man has been a member of seven political parties since he joined politics in 1991 and four political parties (one of which is the PDP which he left and rejoined twice) since 1999. Political wanderer Given this, it is fair to say that he is a political wanderer. Unlike leaders elsewhere, to Atiku, the party is nothing but a vehicle of power that exists for him and he does not exist for the party. It is of course his right to keep trying but this could also be legitimately regarded as an obsession. Nothing is more indicative of that obsession than his attempt to mobilise the governors of the PDP to move against his leader, President Olusegun Obasanjo, a man who had nominated him as his running mate for the second time, topple him as the party’s presidential candidate and take his place as the flag bearer in 2003. This was not only a case of ingratitude but also treachery and especially so because Obasanjo had trusted him to raise all the finances that were needed for that second run. Atiku allegedly raised the money through private donors and then tried to browbeat the President so that he would not be reelected. Two interventions saved Obasanjo. Firstly, the God factor, which was the most important, and, secondly, a stupendously wealthy businessman from Kano (who I shall not name) who made virtually all the money that was needed available for both the delegates at the convention and the election itself. That is how Atiku’s rebellion and ‘Absalom’ agenda was thwarted and crushed. Yet despite that Obasanjo refused to drop him mid-stream as his running mate and he was elected as Vice President on the same ticket of the man that he had sought to humiliate and destroy. Atiku is no Wade It was after the second term began after the 2003 election that the real war between the two camps began and I am proud to say that yours truly and others like Nasir El-Rufai, Nuhu Ribadu, Akin Osuntokun, Abiye Sekibo, Frank Nweke, Uba Sani, Adamu Bello, Julius Ihonvbere and many others that were either working in the Presidency or were Ministers together with others like Peter Odili of Rivers State, Umaru Yar’Adua of Katsina State, Ahmad Makarfi of Kaduna State and a number of other governors took the battle to the gates of the Vice President and gave him hell over the next four years. By the time it was all over, we had put him in his place and proved to him that treachery and rebellion are as the sin of witchcraft and never pay. His political career has not been the same since as he stumbled from one failed bid to the other leaving a legacy of division and destruction in his path. Some may argue that if Abdoulaye Wade of Senegal could eventually win after five attempts Atiku may do so after seven but the truth is that Atiku is no Abdoulaye Wade. He does not have the latter’s sincerity of purpose, courage, sense of loyalty, humility, discipline and patriotism. Outside of that, unlike Wade, Atiku Abubakar is more of a pragmatic businessman who is more interested in rebellion and treachery than a statesman who puts the interest of the nation before his own. Unlike Atiku, Wade would always endeavour to do the right thing by others, especially in the case of those who stood by him. Unlike Atiku, he appreciated the importance of loyalty, he did not covet the position of his leaders, he understood the power and dynamics of patience and he was not one to act desperately. Unlike Atiku, he NEVER tried to undermine, destroy, humiliate, discredit or topple his benefactors and neither did he attempt to dishonour standing agreements or deny others the presidency whenever it was their turn. Wade played politics within the rules and norms: he did not attempt to subvert or violate them to his own advantage. Atiku, on the other hand, revels in subversion and believes that Nigeria was established for his benefit alone. This is a man that has consistently opposed and fought against the idea of power shift to the South ever since he left office in 2007. He enunciated that notion and willingly espoused that grave and grievous injustice. He challenged Goodluck Jonathan in 2011, stayed with the coalition that removed him from power in 2015, took the PDP ticket from Nyesom Wike in 2022, ran against Bola Tinubu and Peter Obi in 2023 and is doing so again in 2027. Contempt for the South What remains striking is that he has done this even in cycles when power shift to the South was the prevailing argument from much of the political class, including many Northern leaders who backed it in the name of rotation, fairness and equity. Clearly, he has contempt for Southern aspirations. That is his mindset though he masks it well. Simply put, he has a sectional outlook and not a national one and for this reason God will not allow him to achieve his ambition. Outside of that, you cannot repay good with evil and escape it before the Lord. Atiku will learn this the hard way and so will those that stand with him. Is it any wonder that this time around he has employed the services of a controversial lobbyist to help him in return for a massive dollar fee? In the history of our country, we have never witnessed a presidential candidate employ foreign publicity firms to openly run down, threaten, slander and disparage the very Nigerians he wants to lead simply because he is so desperate to be President. Yet he will fail and, more importantly,, if the necessary evidence is adduced, he will be made to face the law for alleged corruption when he was Vice President. The most obvious allegation concerns the Mambilla Power Plant case but there are other allegations bordering on the Siemens case, the Halliburton case, the INTELS case, the William J. Jefferson U.S. Congressman case (for which the Congressman went to jail), the Leno Adesanya power plant case (which is reported to have been re-opened) and other serious allegations of corruption and offshore payments involving millions of dollars which, though yet to be proven, have left many unanswered questions. To be fair, none of these cases have, at least so far, resulted in a Nigerian trial or conviction but all have left a paper trail in the files of foreign regulators and many unanswered questions at home. Yet it didn’t stop there. Atiku’s worst crime was not the allegation of financial impropriety but his relentless determination to undermine and destabilise the government that he was elected to serve and to utterly destroy his principal whom he obviously hated with what the Bible described as “a perfect hatred”. Atiku betrayed Obasanjo to such a point that I, as Minister of Aviation at the time, was constrained to demand that he should be thrown out of Cabinet meetings on two separate occasions during full sessions of Cabinet. I did this during the course of the meeting and in the presence of every single Cabinet member and when I did so there was pindrop silence in the Cabinet chambers. The first time, Obasanjo saved him from the humiliation and appealed to me and the other Ministers to allow him to stay whilst he sat there looking daggers at me and clearly in a state of shock. The second time, which was a few weeks later, I made another demand in our Cabinet meeting under ‘other matters’ that if he did not get up and leave the chamber as a consequence of his betrayals and treachery against our President, then we the Ministers would walk out and leave him to conduct the Federal Executive Council meeting alone with the President. Obasanjo again appealed to us to allow him to stay but compelled him to apologise to the entire Cabinet there and then for his treachery and outrageous behaviour all motivated by the fact that he wanted to topple the President and take his place. Atiku apologised there and then to the entire Cabinet and consequently was allowed to stay at the Federal Executive Council meeting but he NEVER attended another Cabinet meeting after that. This episode proves how over-ambitious he was as Vice President and how he coveted the seat of the man that brought him out of obscurity in Adamawa State and made him his Vice President. He repaid Obasanjo’s good with evil just as he later repaid Tinubu’s, Buhari’s and the old PDP’s good with evil in later years. Today he is so desperate to win the presidential election that he has not only destroyed his old party, the PDP, by splitting it into two but he also did the same to the ADC, his new one, by breaking it in two and driving the Obi/Kwankwaso faction out to join a new party called the NDC. Anytime he does not get his way or his ambition to become the flag bearer of whichever party he is in is threatened, the party must be broken. In the case of PDP, he single-handedly killed what was once Nigeria’s dominant party and finally buried it in 2019. That is his political legacy: Chaos and destruction. Subsidy Worse still, as presidential candidate of the ADC, he has said he will restore fuel subsidy just to get votes knowing that in the process of implementing this disastrous policy he will utterly destroy Nigeria and cause us to lose all the economic gains we have made in the last three years. Let him be aware that there is nothing worse than attempting to destroy the future of your people just because you want to be President. Again let him be reminded that to pay a foreign PR company led by a controversial character who uses his wife’s surname rather than his father’s, $1.2 million to denigrate, undermine, demonise, vilify, malign and destroy your President in the international media just because you covet his seat is unacceptable. History is against you Waziri. No person in the world has ever tried to be President of his country seven times or more and has won except for Abdoulaye Wade and, like I said, you are no Wade and neither do you share his gravitas nor have his grit. Statistically and historically, you have little chance of winning on your seventh attempt or of ever becoming President. It appears that the Living God has placed a divine injunction on your ambition. This will be proved in January 2027 when you will be defeated by your old friend and arch-nemesis and be compelled to go back to Dubai and retire in peace. I come in peace, Waziri, and I wish you well. •Chief Femi Fani-Kayode is a former Minister of Culture and Tourism, a former Minister of Aviation, Nigeria’s Ambassador-Designate to South Africa, Lesotho and Estawani, the Sadaukin Shinkafi, the Wakilin Doka Potiskum, the Otunba of Joga Orile, the Aare Ajagunla of Otun Ekiti and a Legal Practitioner The post The 7th bid of Atiku – Fani-Kayode appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Man sentenced to 41-year term for sending 92 nurses abroad on fake papers
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The Federal Investigation Agency (FIA), Islamabad zone, has secured the conviction of two accused involved in sending 92 nurses to Saudi Arabia on fake experience certificates, with the court awarding a total of 41 years’ imprisonment and imposing fines of over Rs9 million on the main culprit. According to FIA and court records, Judge of the Special Court (Central), Rawalpindi, Abdul Rehman Muhammad Arif, pronounced the judgement on Sept 23 in a 2024 case registered under Sections 34/420 /468/471/109 of the Pakistan Penal Code (PPC), read with Sections 18/22 of the Emigration Ordinance (EO) 1979 and Section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act (PCA) 1947. The case pertained to 92 nurses who were sent to Saudi Arabia on fake experience certificates and deported within a month. The FIA said progress in the high-profile case was regularly shared with the PM Office. Accomplice awarded three years rigorous imprisonment According to the warrant of conviction, key agent Ghulam Zulfiqar Ali alias Mian Zulfiqar, son of Din Muhammad, was sentenced to seven years’ rigorous imprisonment (RI) and a Rs100,000 fine, with two months’ further RI in default under Section 420 of PPC; seven years’ RI and a Rs100,000 fine, with two months’ further RI in default under Section 468; seven years’ RI and a Rs100,000 fine, with two months’ further RI in default under Section 471 of PPC; 10 years’ RI and a Rs200,000 fine, with three months’ further RI in default under Section 18 of the Emigration Ordinance 1979; and 10 years’ RI and a Rs200,000 fine, with three months’ further RI in default under Section 22 of the Emigration Ordinance 1979. The total concurrent sentence comes to 41 years, as stated in the FIA infographic. The court further ordered, under Section 544-A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, that convict Zulfiqar Ali pay Rs9.2 million as compensation to the nurses, at Rs100,000 per victim. The amount shall be recovered as arrears of land revenue and, in case of default, the convict shall undergo a further six months’ simple imprisonment. The amount is to be deposited with the FIA Islamabad zone director for disbursement among all 92 victim nurses. The second convict, Ghulam Fareed, son of Muhammad Sadiq, was sentenced to three years’ RI and a Rs200,000 fine under Section 18 of the Emigration Ordinance 1979. However, he was acquitted of charges under Section 22 of the EO, read with Sections 420, 468 and 471 of PPC, by giving him the benefit of the doubt. Published in Dawn, September 27th, 2026

items.title: Zardari urges ethical AI use to boost tourism
items.description: ISLAMABAD: President Asif Ali Zardari has underscored the need to align emerging technologies with ethical tourism frameworks to empower local economies. In his message on the occasion of World Tourism Day 2026, President Zardari welcomed international visitors to explore Pakistan’s diverse landscapes, highlighting a forward-looking vision that blends modern connectivity with traditional values of hospitality. “We have to develop a tourism sector that embraces innovation while remaining rooted in our values of hospitality, respect and responsibility,” President Zardari said. Says digital technology is reshaping how people plan and experience travel This year’s theme, “Digital Agenda and Artificial Intelligence to Redesign Tourism”, draws attention to the changes that technology and artificial intelligence are bringing to the way people plan their journeys, discover destinations and experience different cultures. “We must ensure that these changes remain responsible, inclusive and beneficial to people and communities,” Mr Zardari said. “Pakistan has a remarkable diversity of landscapes and experiences, from the mountains of the north and the ancient civilisations of the Indus Valley to our Islamic and Gandhara heritage, cities, deserts and coastal areas. Our greatest strength, however, remains the warmth and hospitality of our people,” he said. According to the president, tourism can create livelihoods, support local businesses and open opportunities for young people and women. It can also bring economic activity to communities across the country. “At the same time, we must protect our natural environment, cultural heritage and traditions for future generations,” he said. Published in Dawn, September 27th, 2026

items.title: Mid-Autumn Festival sees vibrant cultural activities, tourism spending
items.description: China's Mid-Autumn Festival, observed on the 15th day of the eighth month of the Chinese lunar calendar, is one of the country's most important traditional festivals. Centered on the full moon, the festival symbolizes reunion and togetherness, with families gathering to share meals, admire the moon and enjoy traditional customs. As China celebrates the Mid-Autumn Festival, the three-day holiday is highlighting both the enduring appeal of traditional culture and the vitality of domestic consumption, with a wide range of festive activities and tourism offerings bringing new momentum to the holiday economy. Across the country, people are embracing the festival with colorful celebrations, from traditional performances and lantern displays to moon-viewing activities. Data from third-party travel platforms showed that Chinese-style nighttime tourism was especially popular on the first day of the holiday. The holiday also saw a travel peak as demand for family visits coincided with short-distance getaways. China State Railway Group said 17.139 million passenger trips were made by rail nationwide on the first day of the Mid-Autumn holiday, with railway operations remaining safe and orderly. Average daily traffic on China's expressways was expected to reach about 41 million vehicles during the holiday, the Ministry of Transport's road network center estimated. Online travel platforms showed that intercity travel bookings for departures on the day before and the first day of the holiday rose 18% from the same period during this year's Dragon Boat Festival holiday, another three-day public holiday in China. Short-distance trips remained dominant, with bookings for local and nearby destinations accounting for more than 60% of total holiday travel. Beyond tourism, family reunions remained at the heart of the festival, with dining and gatherings emerging as another major driver of holiday consumption. Online lifestyle service data showed that orders related to Mid-Autumn reunion dinners surged more than 105% year on year.

items.title: Why Makinde wants 2027 to be ‘APC VS. Nigerians’
items.description: By Luminous Jannamike Governor Seyi Makinde of Oyo wants Nigerians to look at the 2027 presidential election and see something bigger than another contest between political parties.He wants them to see the ruling All Progressives Congress, APC, on one side and Nigerians on the other. That was the striking message the governor carried to Katsina last Tuesday, where he declared: “It won’t be APC versus APM, or APM versus ADC, or ADC versus NDC. It will be APC versus Nigerians.” The choice of words was significant. Makinde is the presidential candidate of the Allied Peoples Movement, APM, yet he is deliberately refusing to make APM the immediate centre of his argument. Instead, he is trying to make the election a referendum on the party controlling the Federal Government; and on whether Nigerians want to give it another four years. It is a potentially useful calculation for a candidate whose party does not have the national political machinery of the ruling APC. But it also carries a difficult question: if the election becomes a contest between APC and dissatisfied Nigerians, why should those Nigerians necessarily choose APM? That is the political gamble behind Makinde’s Katsina message. Changing the question Makinde appears to understand that a conventional party-versus-party contest could force APM to spend too much of the campaign explaining itself before it can challenge the incumbent. An anti-APC contest changes that equation. Instead of asking voters first to embrace APM, Makinde wants them to ask whether they are satisfied with the APC government. If the answer is no, his campaign then has to present his ticket as the vehicle through which that dissatisfaction can be converted into votes. His criticism of President Bola Tinubu’s handling of his recent absence from the country fits neatly into that strategy. Makinde invoked Section 145 of the Constitution and compared presidential conduct with his own practice in Oyo State. “I have looked at the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria and, of course, as a state governor, I also operate under that Constitution. Anytime I have to travel out, not for work but on vacation, for more than 21 days, I transmit power to the Deputy Governor. Why is this not happening at the national level?” Makinde said. Section 145(1) requires the President, when proceeding on vacation or otherwise unable to discharge his functions, to transmit a written declaration to the Senate President and Speaker of the House. The 21-day provision in subsection 2 concerns what the National Assembly may do if such a declaration has not been transmitted within that period. It does not mean the President’s obligation begins after 21 days. Makinde then turned the constitutional argument into a promise about how he would govern. “I promise you that, as your President, I will follow the Constitution to the letter. If I am not going to be available, if I am on vacation, I will transmit power to the Vice President. Record this and hold me accountable,” he said. The significance of the argument is less about the length of the President’s absence than the political frame Makinde is constructing: a government that must account for its decisions, comply with the Constitution and explain its actions to citizens. The same approach runs into the economy. The Federal Government says the removal of the petrol subsidy and foreign-exchange reforms have created additional fiscal space. Finance Minister Taiwo Oyedele said subsidy savings between June 2023 and December 2025 amounted to N15.8 trillion, while incremental Federal Government resources reached N20.4 trillion. But for households confronting higher prices and living costs, the question is what those savings mean in daily life. That gives Makinde another opening. He can accept the argument that the reforms have increased government resources while asking whether those resources have translated sufficiently into security, jobs, infrastructure and purchasing power. His objective is to turn that gap into a political question about the APC. The 2023 warning The North-West is particularly important to that calculation. In Katsina, Atiku Abubakar defeated Tinubu by 6,762 votes in 2023, polling 489,045 votes against Tinubu’s 482,283. Rabiu Kwankwaso received 69,386 votes. Across the North-West, Atiku won Kaduna, Katsina, Kebbi and Sokoto; Tinubu carried Jigawa and Zamfara, while Kwankwaso won Kano. The figures do not automatically translate into support for Makinde. What they demonstrate is something more basic: the APC’s hold on the region is not uniform, and the presidential vote can be divided among competing political forces. That makes the region useful territory for a candidate attempting to construct an anti-incumbency coalition. Makinde’s challenge, however, is to make that coalition belong to him. His running mate, Lawal Daura, is part of that calculation. APM National Chairman Dantele presented Daura as a North-West answer to the security crisis. “We have your own son from the North-West, particularly Katsina, the Vice presidential candidate, Lawal Daura who is a security guru and he will be there to address security challenges across the North-West and Nigeria at large,” Dantele said. “Let our farmers return to their farms. Let our children go to school freely. Let Nigerians coexist peacefully and go about their normal businesses. We must put an end to insecurity and hunger, improve access to education, and eradicate poverty.” Daura himself described the mood the ticket hopes to exploit. “The North-West, and indeed Nigeria at large, is yearning for reseting Nigeria,” Daura said. The ticket is therefore trying to combine two appeals: Makinde as the face of governance and institutional change, and Daura as the North-West connection with security placed at the centre of the regional pitch. But the campaign still has to move from political symbolism to policy. Calling Daura a ‘security guru’ does not by itself explain how the ticket would protect farmers, schools and communities, reform policing or finance a broader security architecture. That gap becomes important because the argument is not simply that APC should be rejected. Makinde must also demonstrate what comes after the rejection. The problem with an anti-APC election This is where Makinde’s strategy becomes more complicated. The APC can be made the target without APM becoming the automatic beneficiary. A voter can be unhappy with the ruling party and still choose another opposition platform. Indeed, the more the election is framed as a referendum on APC, the greater the number of political actors that can attempt to capture the resulting dissatisfaction. Makinde therefore needs to perform two political operations at once. First, he has to persuade Nigerians that the election is fundamentally about the record of the APC government. Then he has to persuade those same voters that APM is the vehicle through which they should express their verdict. His appeal for voters to obtain their Permanent Voter Cards reflects that calculation. “Please get your PVC and show the APC that Nigeria is bigger than individuals. It is bigger than even the systems that have held us down,” Makinde said. The language deliberately puts the voter ahead of the party. But there is a second message beneath it: That citizens can punish the ruling party through the ballot box. The unresolved question is where that punishment ultimately lands. Selling the Alternative This is why Makinde’s record in Oyo State matters to the strategy. If he only campaigns against Tinubu, he risks becoming another opposition politician asking voters to reject the incumbent without establishing why his own ticket should receive their support. His Oyo record gives him something with which to answer that question. The state’s 2024 budget stood at N434.2 billion, with projected internally generated revenue of N72 billion. Education received N90.65 billion, representing about 20.88 per cent of the budget. The Oyo government also reported 118.07 kilometres of roads delivered in the year preceding its 2025 budget presentation, including 76.67 kilometres of the Iseyin-Fapote-Ogbomoso Road. Those figures provide Makinde with a record to put beside his criticism of the Federal Government. But the presidential argument inevitably becomes harder at that point. Running Oyo is different from running a federation responsible for defence, foreign affairs, monetary policy and the distribution of federal resources. So the next stage of Makinde’s campaign cannot simply be about making APC unpopular. It has to establish that his proposed ‘reset’ can operate at federal scale. That is why his promise to return to the North-West matters. “This is the town hall for the Northwest. I am still coming back here in Katsina, Kaduna, Kano, Kebbi, Zamfara and Jigawa to campaign on a state-by-state basis,” Makinde said. He is effectively taking the argument beyond Katsina: APC may be the target, but APM wants to be the beneficiary. That is the central calculation behind the phrase ‘APC versus Nigerians’. Makinde is trying to remove the election from the familiar terrain of party labels and place the ruling party’s record at the centre of the ballot. The strategy gives him a larger potential constituency than APM alone can provide. But it also creates the campaign’s biggest unanswered question. If Nigerians decide that 2027 should indeed be about APC versus them, Makinde still has to convince them that when they cast that anti-incumbency vote, APM is where it should land. The post Why Makinde wants 2027 to be ‘APC VS. Nigerians’ appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.description: L’ancien Premier ministre guinéen et président de l’Union des forces républicaines (UFR), Sidya Touré, est décédé vendredi 25 septembre 2026 à Paris, à l’âge de 81 ans. Deux fois candidat à l’élection présidentielle, il vivait ces dernières années en exil à Abidjan et n’aura pas pu revoir son pays avant sa mort.
