items.title: Tinubu is my friend but I don’t like the direction he’s taking Nigeria –Donald Duke
items.description: • Joins subsidy debate, says petrol can sell at N200 • Insists ‘Lagos-Calabar Highway is fancy road, we don’t need it now’ By Soni Daniel, Northern Region Editor “President Tinubu is my friend. But I disagree with the direction he’s taking Nigeria. Even within a family, we all don’t have to think and act the same way”. With these words, Mr. Donald Duke, a former governor of Cross River State (1999 – 2027, same time Tinubu was governor of Lagos State), explains, in this interview, why he is challenging Tinubu in the 2027 elections. Duke is vying in the election on the platform of the Peoples Redemption Party (PRP). He also speaks on the very contentious issue of the removal of petrol subsidy and the position of former VP Atiku Abubakar to restore the subsidy if elected president in 2027 among other issues in the polity. Excerpts: ADC presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar, said if elected, he would return fuel subsidy to reduce the burden on Nigerians. What would you do in this regard if you become president? I don’t believe there should be subsidy and I have spoken on this in several forums. If, for instance, you buy water at N10 and Nigerians cannot afford to pay N10 for it, and you decide that you’re going to give them at N5, then you’re subsidizing the water. That’s the ordinary meaning of subsidy. If you have a borehole in your compound and you’re producing 200,000 litres of water for sale and you decide to keep maybe 20,000 for your farm use and then sell the balance, you cannot come back and say you are doing subsidy. This is how people look at the subsidy. But I don’t believe in subsidy. This oil is our own, right? It belongs to all of us. It’s our common wealth. Don’t look at the price of the oil in the international market. We need about 300,000 barrels a day. We produce about 1.7m barrels, okay? We sell about 1.4 barrels commercially. The 300,000, look at the cost of production, not the international price. While we sell crude oil at today $70 or $80 a barrel, the cost of production may not exceed $40 a barrel, okay? A barrel of crude in Nigeria has about seven byproducts. Of those seven byproducts, the key ones to us are probably diesel and PMS, petrol. The others are aviation fuel, kerosene. Diesel and petrol are the key ones, let government give them to us at the cost of production, not at the market price but take into cognizance the cost of distribution and put 5% or 10% above, right? Sell the five other byproducts from a barrel of crude at commercial rates. If this is done, you would find that you can easily amortize this petrol, and give it to your people at N200 or N300 per litre. Why is it important? That’s what drives your economy. That’s what drives the country, right? You’ve got to use what you’ve got to get what you want. China did so in its early days. Southeast Asia and Japan used cheap labor when they were developing. Cambodia and many other countries use cheap labour to make clothes for export and they are doing well. They’re using what they’ve got. China today is not cheap labor anymore because they’ve developed, right? In Nigeria’s case, oil is what gives us an edge over others. Our economic advantage is our energy. But we are flaring gas. There was a time Nigeria was flaring 2.5 billion cubic feet of gas daily. You can’t imagine it. That’s the equivalent of 25 million litres of diesel. Can you imagine what 25 million litres of diesel is? They just burn it. And we did it for many decades. But it has been significantly reduced But the reduction is that they’ve ingested it into the ground, not that they’re using it for anything. So why don’t you spend the money, clean the gas, and make sure that there’s a gas point in every senatorial district? Nigeria should not sell its gas for local consumption at international price. It’s your own. Just sell it at a point where you know that you can keep production going. That’s why I said when you calculate everything, add maybe 10%. I’m not saying sell it as a loss that you can say you’re subsidizing. Sell it at the cost of production because it’s yours. Don’t come and tell me that gas in Nigeria is cheaper than America or cheaper than England. You’re not where they are. Those are not your mates. How can you say, for instance, that this is the price of a product that keeps your economy going, but most people cannot afford it, and you own it? It’s not that you’re getting it from another country. It’s your own. It doesn’t make sense. Then they turn around and say, “oh, if it’s so cheap, it will find its way across the borders”. So, are you going to punish your people because you can’t police your borders? And why don’t you think of a solution to that? Okay, you can dye your oil and petrol. You can say petrol from Nigeria is purple, blue, yellow, red, whatever. It’s a dye. It doesn’t affect the car, the engine, you know. So, if you find that color petrol in Chad or Niger, you know it came from Nigeria and the security agencies can track and arrest those taking the fuel across the borders. They should go and find out how Nigeria’s petrol got to such places and deal with those responsible for the theft. That’s how it works. But you can’t punish your people because the essence of governance is to ensure that the people are productive. That’s why we go to school. That’s why we have hospitals. If you’re sick, you’re not productive. But the Bretton Woods people are subsidising food. Yeah, nobody’s talking about that. You’ve got to keep your people productive. If there’s no food, right, they cannot survive. So, they make it available. That is why I am saying that whatever keeps your people alive and you have in abundance, use it. I don’t know why it’s so difficult. I’ve sat down with three or four finance ministers. They don’t get it. They all want to please the World Bank and IMF, but the people in the World Bank and IMF are just like us. Small, small boys that go to Harvard and all these schools, you know. Some are there telling Nigeria what to do. When I was in school, these people were not born. But today they’re advising Nigeria how to run the economy. You’ve got to be productive. The essence of government, like I said, is to ensure that all of us are productive. If all of us are productive, the environment is safe and there’s order. What more does government do? That’s all the government is. You know, my definition is, the reason why we need government is for the utmost productivity of our citizens within a safe and orderly environment. That’s why you need security. That’s why you have the judiciary. You want to make the environment orderly and safe. That’s it. If Nigeria was safe and orderly and people are productive, who cares whether you’re from Sokoto or from this, you know. Nobody cares. Because we’re all doing one thing or the other. But where inadequacy persists because we’re not productive, we begin to use tribal sentiments or want to take advantage of it to achieve what we want to achieve. So, if I’m a Calabar man and I find that the man in this office who can give me what I need is a Calabar man in the military, I start speaking Efik to him because I want to appeal to that sentiment. Or if I’m a Christian, right, I start saying Jesus saves, or Muslim I try to appeal to that sentiment to get what I want. I don’t believe that we’re tribalistic or we’re ethnic. We just use things because it is advantageous to us. So, we want a president or a governor from our locality because we think it will give you added advantage, right? But if you’re getting everything without that added advantage, who cares where the governor comes from? You’re not looking at merit. After all, when you go to hospital, you don’t ask for the doctor who is from your village. You ask for the doctor who can cure you. So, I don’t believe there’s ethnicity. It’s because of inadequacy that we try and use what we’ve got to get what we want. Why is the cost of living in Nigeria so high? What went wrong and how did we get here? I think we got it wrong right from independence and as the years go by, the effects become starker. We have not addressed the issue of productivity. I use an example which is like a broken record, but I’ll say it here. Between 1979 and 1983, Shehu Shagari was president. His average budget for those four years was $25 billion. Our population in the mid-70s was about 76 million people. Today, our population, they say, is about 230 million people. We’re still spending the same $25 billion that Shagari spent 46 years ago. All the trillions, by the time you divide it, you come down to the same thing. So, in essence, the economy has not grown. In fact, it has shrunk because $25 billion in 1979 or 1980 is not the same as today. So, the economy has shrunk, and people just need to survive. So, they’re going to banditry and kidnapping to make a living. The Boko Haram crisis is caused by poverty. And once they taste that kind of money, it’s very difficult to wean them off it. So, a kidnapper kidnaps someone and gets 20 million Naira. You tell him to go and do a steady job, they’ll give him N250,000 Naira. It can’t work because the villain has already tasted blood. When I was in university, we had Maitatsine crisis, which came before Boko Haram and all that. And it was always from that Maiduguri area, in the northeastern part, which is the poorest part of the North. So, you find that those things are exacerbated from those parts. Now, it’s creeping all over the North and coming down South. That’s on one hand. On the other hand is the clear fact that we have not really updated our security architecture since the end of the Civil War in 1970. It’s only recently that they created more Divisions, right? But you notice something. In the United States, they have what they call the National Guard, which is military and is in every state. Yes. The National Guard is really like having a Division of the military in every state. So, they’ve really decentralized security. And I’ll say something here for free. Anything that is essential must be local. So, you have to localize the security to take care of everything everywhere in the country. Due to the fact that 80% of security is intelligence, nobody should stay in Sokoto and want to know what it is. I think if you have the local intelligence in Calabar, you need the local people there to gather that intelligence for you to use and enforce. Don’t forget that only 20% of policing is enforcement, while 80% is intelligence gathering. So, we need to start thinking differently. That’s why at the introduction, I said we must have a collective vision. Where are we taking this country to? We don’t have a vision. We just wake up and do whatever is important. We woke up one morning and said we want to build a road from Lagos to Calabar. Nobody thought about the economics? Nobody thought about how many communities we would need to go through . If a road just goes straight from Lagos to Calabar with nothing in-between, of what value is that? I would be the happiest person because I live in Lagos and Calabar. So, I would be going back and forth. But a road is a commuting infrastructure between communities. There are existing roads. You and I know that if, I don’t believe they’ll get to Calabar, but let’s assume they get to Calabar. What happens to the other roads? What happens to the East-west highway that we’ve been talking about? You know that nobody will pay attention to them. Even if it were the best road to be a sea view, you want to be looking at the sea as you’re going to Calabar, fine. What is the economics of it? What is the opportunity cost? Maybe you can say “we’ll do it in 10 years when we can afford it”. But we can’t afford it now. There are higher priorities. Children are out of school. We have the largest number of out-of-school children in the world. We have the largest number of poor people in the world. And you’re building a fancy road from Victoria Island to Calabar? It doesn’t work like that. So, all I’m asking for is let’s be honest with our people. Somalia is a country that has no ethnic group. They are all one ethnic group and one religion. It’s mono-ethnic, mono-religion and they are fighting. Why are they fighting? Poverty is the cause of the fighting! The people are simply poor. This is a mono-ethnic and mono-religious society. One of the few in all of Africa where all of them come from the same ethnic group, they are Somalis. That’s their ethnic group. But how would you tackle rising insecurity in the land? We will have to deliberately decentralise policing. The idea of state police, even local government police, is right. Have it. Have the guidelines, but you must strengthen the judiciary. This is because there must be someone that everyone reports to if things go wrong. But the idea of having it is not bad. After all, the national police system is also abused by the president. You know? Yes. It’s not the governors only. Set it up. Put stringent guidelines. Right? Their main preoccupation should be intelligence gathering. It’s a shame that after almost 20 years of Boko Haram, we don’t have any intelligence on them. We have not infiltrated their ranks. We ought to have infiltrated their ranks by now to know what they will do next. Why did you choose PRP given that it is not a popular vehicle? Tell me a better vehicle. Huh? Tell me a better vehicle. If you go to Kano, you hear of PRP. That’s not the point. I told you my aim is very difficult to say a PRP will win the national elections. But I told you I want to be in the field of discussion. Right? I want to change the trajectory of our discussion. A lot of younger people are losing hope because nobody is discussing what gives them hope for tomorrow. Nobody. So, I want to be there. But let me tell you something directly about your question. Where was NDC six months ago? Where was ADC six months ago? There are new contraptions. But I believe that regardless of all these contraptions, for presidential democracy to work now, we all have to come together. Why are you not joining the 1999-2007 set of governors to support the incumbent president? We all don’t have to be. President Tinubu is my friend. But I disagree with the direction he’s taking Nigeria. Even within a family, we all don’t have to think and act the same way. Even in Atiku’s family, I hear one of his sons is an APC (member). We don’t have to be in one party. And that’s the beauty of democracy. We express ourselves. items.title: Igbo leaders reject Abuja restructuring communiqué
items.description: •Propose 10-region structure, resource control, regional police By Nnamdi Ojiego Barely four months to the 2027 general elections, Igbo leaders, under the umbrella of Igbo Leaders of Thought, ILT, have called for the temporary suspension of elections pending the completion of Nigeria’s restructuring exercise. This came as the leaders proposed a 10-region political structure while rejecting the communiqué issued at the Abuja restructuring conference of August 20, 2026. The group, which also demanded the unconditional release of the detained leader of the Indigenous People of Biafra, IPOB, Nnamdi Kanu, said the restructuring exercise should be concluded before May 2027, with elections subsequently conducted under the new constitutional arrangement. It also insisted on the creation of a united Igbo Region extending to the Atlantic coast, incorporating Abia, Anambra, Ebonyi, Enugu, Imo, prospective Anioma, Rivers State and Igbo communities in parts of Akwa Ibom, Bayelsa, Benue, Cross River, Edo and Kogi states. The position was contained in a statement titled, ‘Igbo Position on the Restructuring of Nigeria,’ dated September 16, 2026, and published in newspapers. It was signed by Emeritus Prof. Elochukwu Amucheazi, President-General of the ILT; Sen. John Azuta-Mbata, President-General of Ohanaeze Ndigbo; Prof. Dozie, Chukwuokolo, Secretary-General, ILT; Amb. Uche Ajulu-Okeke, adviser Igbo delegation; Dr. Katchi Ononuju, deputy leader Igbo delegation; and Prof. Obasi Igwe, leader of Igbo delegation to the Abuja conference. The organisation said restructuring was necessary to address what it described as the country’s foundational problems, arguing that the 1914 amalgamation was imposed without the consent of the constituent nationalities. It said: “By 2014 many had come to the understanding that the problem is foundational: that the non-consensual nature of the ‘union’ would continue to make it a violent, shaky and largely unproductive experiment; that with an anachronistic basis the superstructure would sooner or later eventually collapse.” The group added that “instead of the exercise in futility that inheres in building from the top, it is more rational to build from below, so as to have a better and stable constitutive union of the people than an imposed arrangement from above benefiting only a few.” It said restructuring should be based on ethno-linguistic cultural groups, adding that granting such groups some degree of self-determination would lay the foundation for peaceful coexistence and address the national question. Suspension of elections On the timing of the exercise, the ILT proposed that restructuring should be concluded before May 2027, with elections temporarily suspended until the process was completed. Under its general principles of restructuring, the group stated: “Duration of restructuring exercise should conclude before May 2027, with elections temporarily put on hold by an act of necessity, and resumed on post-restructuring principles.” The group said the restructuring process should enable Nigerians to determine the political and constitutional arrangement they desired through regional or nationwide referendums. It stated that it supported “the right to self-determination for Nigeria’s ethnic nationalities, regardless of size,” and upheld the principle that regions should be based on “ethno-linguistic civilizations or groupings thereof.” Kanu’s release The ILT also called for the immediate listing of Kanu’s long-delayed court case for accelerated hearing and his unconditional release. It said the release and rehabilitation of political prisoners, particularly Kanu and his colleagues, would help build confidence and trust in discussions on Nigeria’s future. “The Igbo see in the unconditional release and rehabilitation of all political prisoners, above all Mazi Nnamdi Kanu and his colleagues, as maintained by the Igbo delegation at the recent Abuja Conference, as a gateway to mutual trust and confidence in discussions on the future of Nigeria.” It also renewed its support for regional referendums or a nationwide referendum conducted by an independent body to enable Nigerians decide on the country’s future constitutional arrangement. Proposed 10-region structure The organisation proposed a 10-region structure to replace the existing states, local government areas and geopolitical zones, with five coastal regions in the South and five riparian regions in the North. “Regions based on single-ethnic or consenting multi-ethnic nationalities, to replace States, LGAS, Geopolitical Zones, North, South, East, West, etc paradigms. 5 coastal Regions in the South and 5 riparian Regions in the North are proposed by the Igbo, with relevant maps.” On resource control, it stated: “Resource ownership and control reverts to the Regions, which would fund the centre on agreed terms.” The group also proposed military and security reorganisation to achieve a balance between the regions, saying regional police should be one element of a broader security arrangement. It said: “Military-security reorganization to achieve security balance between Regions, of which Regional police is only one element. On the proposed distribution of powers, the ILT said it supported the abolition of the concurrent legislative list, with exclusive and residual powers retained by the federal and regional governments respectively. It further proposed a mixed private-public free enterprise economy and a secular political system, with religion separated from the state and political affairs. The organisation said all southern regions should have contiguous access to the coast and retain their traditional coastal ports, while northern regions should border either the Niger or Benue rivers. It stated that the three proposed Middle Belt regions could merge into one or two, while portions of the South could merge with the Igbo or Yoruba regions to create larger eastern or western regions and reduce the number of regions. The post Igbo leaders reject Abuja restructuring communiqué appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Eight terrorists killed in Dera Bugti clash, police claim
items.description: • Peace force member martyred, three injured; seven ‘terrorists’ arrested • Tribal leader shot dead in Khuzdar; Bizenjo’s residence attacked QUETTA/KHUZDAR: At least eight suspected terrorists were killed in a clash with the Bugti Peace Force, a pro-government tribal militia, in the Loti area of Dera Bugti district on Saturday, according to police officials. A policeman who was part of the peace force was martyred and three other members were injured during the clash. Separately, a tribal leader was killed in the Naal area of Khuzdar and firing was also reported at the residence of Sardar Aslam Bizenjo, a central leader of the National Party, in the same area. Police officials said that following the clash, the peace force arrested seven suspected terrorists who allegedly belonged to a banned outfit. Sources said armed men attacked the residence of Dera Bugti District Council Chairman Ghulam Nabi Shambani and a gas company camp in the Loti area of Dera Bugti district with heavy weapons in the early hours of Saturday. The Bugti Peace Force personnel, who were deployed for the protection of the district council chairman and the gas company camp, took positions and returned fire. An exchange of fire continued for over an hour, during which heavy weapons, including rockets, were used by both sides. Some attackers were killed in the exchange of fire. Sources said that after the heavy exchange of fire, some attackers escaped from the site. However, they returned later in the day and again attacked the residence of the Dera Bugti district council chairman, who is close to Balochistan Chief Minister Sarfraz Bugti. The sources added that eight attackers were killed in the exchange of fire while seven others were arrested by the peace force. Their bodies were shifted to Loti hospital. “A member of the peace force identified as Fazal Khan lost his life as he suffered multiple bullet injuries,” a police official said. “Three other members of the peace force, who were injured in the clash, were shifted to a hospital,” he added. The official said further action and investigation into the incident were underway. Tribal leader shot dead Meanwhile, a tribal leader, Sardar Ghulam Nabi Siyahpad, was gunned down by unidentified attackers in the Naal area of Khuzdar district. Police officials said the attackers, riding motorcycles, opened fire on the tribal leader while he was sitting outside his house in the evening. He sustained multiple bullet wounds and died at the spot, while the attackers fled. In a separate incident, unidentified men opened fire at the residence of National Party central leader and former provincial minister Sardar Muhammad Aslam Bizenjo in Naal town, injuring one of his security guards. “Sardar Bizenjo was not present in the house at the time,” a police officer said. Police launched investigations into the incidents. No group has so far claimed responsibility for either attack. The National Party’s Khuzdar district chapter condemned the firing on Sardar Bizenjo’s residence and demanded an immediate, transparent and impartial investigation. In a statement, the party’s district spokesperson said targeting the residence of a political and tribal leader was a matter of concern and urged the authorities to ensure effective security for Mr Bizenjo, his family and residence. The National Party expressed solidarity with Mr Bizenjo and his family and prayed for the early recovery of the injured security guard. Published in Dawn, September 27th, 2026

items.title: 10m beneficiaries of cash transfers don’t have phones, not on social media – APC Chairman
items.description: By Ayobami Okerinde The National Chairman of the All Progressives Congress (APC), Nentawe Yilwatda, says more than 10 million vulnerable Nigerians who benefited from the N75,000 conditional cash transfer programme do not have access to mobile phones or social media. Yilwatda disclosed this on Saturday while speaking with journalists after a three-day retreat of the APC National Executive Council in Maiduguri, Borno State. The beneficiaries, whom he described as poor and vulnerable Nigerians, were largely unable to participate in public discussions about government policies because they lacked access to phones, television and social media. “We have given 75,000 naira to over 10 million Nigerians across the country using the conditional cash transfer under the Ministry of Humanitarian Affairs and Poverty Reduction. “Mind you, these people who are poor and vulnerable don’t have telephones to make calls; they are not on social media. They don’t have a television. They cannot come and challenge and discuss as we are doing here, but they are out there,” he said. Yilwatda also criticised former Vice President and African Democratic Congress presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar, over his position on the fuel subsidy. “We are constructing roads and paying people that are working on the road site, and construction is going across the country,” he said. “Over 30 states could not pay salaries and pensions. After we removed subsidies, all states can pay salaries and pensions, and no state is left behind. “Today, if you return it, you are saying states shouldn’t pay salaries again. And what suffering are you bringing to Nigeria?” The APC chairman also argued that a return to fuel subsidy would affect the government’s student loan scheme and other projects. “The projects we’re doing across the country, like the coastal road and gas project to the north, which have passed Abuja, which are aimed at easing the suffering of Nigerians, will be suspended,” he said. Yilwatda further accused Atiku of seeking to reverse the gains of the Tinubu administration in pursuit of the presidency, saying the APC and Nigerians would not accept such a move. The APC chairman said the NEC retreat also reviewed the party’s activities at the national, state, local government, ward and polling-unit levels. According to him, the party concluded that it remained strong and prepared for the 2027 general elections. He said the NEC passed a vote of confidence in President Bola Tinubu, Vice President Kashim Shettima and other APC candidates who emerged from the party’s primaries for the 2027 elections. items.title: Mad rush into deadly pits for gold: 374 illegal mining sites in 17 states uncovered
items.description: •Reports say 156 dead •NASS C’ttee: This is a sophisticated national threat…with implications for security, revenue generation •How it fuels child labour By Shina Abubakar, Femi Bolaji, Ibrahim Hassan-Wuyo, Golok Nanmwa, Jeff Agbodo, James Ogunnaike and Deola Badru Illegal mining, an economic and environmental offence, has assumed a more troubling dimension in Nigeria, with security agencies, regulators and community leaders increasingly warning that the illicit exploitation of the country’s mineral resources is becoming a national security concern. In parts of the North-West and North-Central, the activity has intersected with banditry, kidnapping and other forms of organised crime, while in other parts of the country, it is fuelling conflicts over land, destroying farmlands and forests, polluting water sources and leaving behind dangerous mining pits. Recently, the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps, NSCDC, which has responsibility for the Mining Marshals, described illegal mining as a major national security threat, saying the problem had gone beyond an economic crime and required intelligence-driven and coordinated enforcement. Concern The concern has also reached the National Assembly, with the House of Representatives Committee on Mineral Exploitation, Security and Anti-Money Laundering describing illegal mining as a “sophisticated national threat” with far-reaching implications for security, revenue generation, environmental sustainability and governance. Concerned by the situation, the Federal Government responded with a combination of enforcement, prosecution and attempts to formalise artisanal mining. However, concerns remain over the effectiveness of these measures. Accordingly, Mining Marshals, established under the NSCDC, have been deployed across the country to identify and shut illegal sites, arrest suspects and protect licensed mining areas. Last month, the Minister of Solid Minerals Development, Dele Alake, said the Mining Marshals had identified 374 illegal mining sites, cleared 108, arrested 743 suspects and prosecuted 165 cases involving 430 accused persons, with five convictions secured. Operations Also, NSCDC reported hundreds of arrests and the shutdown of numerous illegal sites, insisting that its operations are increasingly based on intelligence gathering and collaboration with other security and regulatory agencies. But the actors behind the illicit trade are not limited to rural miners who wield shovels and pickaxes at the sites. Checks by Sunday Vanguard showed a multilayered chain involving artisanal miners, labourers, mineral buyers, middlemen, financiers, processors and, in some cases, foreign nationals. The authorities have particularly raised concerns about the participation of some foreigners in unauthorised mining and mineral trading. In May 2026, Alake disclosed that more than 327 people, including foreign nationals, had been apprehended for illegal mining, with some cases involving suspected links to terrorism handed over to the Office of the National Security Adviser for further investigation. He said the government had also revoked about 3,000 mining licences as part of efforts to sanitise the sector. Among the foreign nationals repeatedly appearing in recent enforcement operations are Chinese nationals. In May, the NSCDC Mining Marshals arraigned 15 Chinese nationals and nine Nigerians before the Federal High Court in Abuja over alleged illegal lithium mining in Kokona Local Government Area of Nasarawa State. In September, four Chinese nationals were arrested in Maiya’aki, Lapai Local Government Area of Niger State, over alleged unauthorised mining activities at a site where they reportedly had no valid licences. Earlier, an EFCC court filing alleged that Chinese and Nigerian nationals were involved in the illegal extraction and trading of mica and lithium, with some of the minerals allegedly moved to Ogun State for processing and export through Lagos. Character Sunday Vanguard observed that the scale and character of illegal mining vary from state to state. In Zamfara, gold mining has intersected with banditry and other forms of insecurity. In Plateau, unsafe mining practices have been linked to repeated deaths, while Taraba has witnessed repeated government orders suspending mining activities. In Osun, illegal gold mining has been associated with environmental degradation and clashes involving enforcement personnel. Nasarawa has emerged as a major lithium-mining frontier, attracting both local and foreign operators, while in Benue, mining activities have taken place alongside displacement and insecurity. State-by-state findings revealed the locations of mining activities, the minerals involved, the actors operating in the sector, the environmental consequences, reported deaths and the response of governments and security agencies. ZAMFARA: Gold, banditry Illegal gold mining remains a major concern in Zamfara State, particularly around Maru, Anka, Bukkuyum, Talata Mafara and Zurmi. Not every miner operating in these areas is involved in criminal activity. Many rural residents depend on artisanal mining for income. However, security concerns become more pronounced where unregulated mining overlaps with armed groups and weak state control. In April 2025, an attack in Gobirawar Chali, Maru Local Government Area, reportedly left at least 19 people dead, while Amnesty International said more than 20 people were killed. There have also been reports alleging that a terror kingpin demanded protection levies from gold miners in Zurmi. The allegations could not be independently verified. In September 2025, a mining pit collapsed in Kadauri, Maru Local Government Area, with reports indicating casualties, although the exact number was not immediately established. The environmental consequences have also been serious, with mining activities affecting farmland and vegetation and raising concerns about the pollution of water sources. Despite repeated enforcement operations, illegal mining has persisted, highlighting the challenge of combining surveillance and enforcement with formalisation and alternative livelihoods for communities dependent on artisanal mining. NIGER: Gold, multiple minerals Illegal and unauthorised mining activities have been reported across several parts of Niger State, including Lapai, Katcha, Kontagora, Mariga, Minna, Shiroro, Rafi, Suleja, Agwara, Borgu, Munya and Paikoro. Gold mining is particularly prominent in areas including Minna, Kontagora, Rafi, Paikoro, Magama and Shiroro, while the state also has deposits of talc, feldspar, iron ore, beryl, amethyst, tourmaline, graphite, kyanite, manganese, mica, wolframite, marble, lead, copper and topaz. In Lapai, four Chinese nationals were arrested in September 2026 at Maiya’aki over alleged unauthorised mining activities. Similar concerns have been raised in Katcha, including the Zuzungi area, where alleged unauthorised mining by Chinese nationals attracted enforcement attention. Authorities have also shut down mineral-processing sites in Kontagora as part of efforts to curb illegal activities. The state came under national attention in September 2026 after 37 suspected illegal miners died while in NSCDC custody. The circumstances surrounding the deaths are under investigation, while the Federal Government has constituted an independent 10-member committee to investigate the incident. PLATEAU: Multiple disasters, deaths Plateau State has witnessed a succession of mining-related accidents, attacks and other incidents resulting in significant loss of lives. Mining activities are concentrated in areas including Barkin Ladi, Jos South, Bassa, Riyom, Wase, Bokkos and Mangu. In November 2024, 13 people reportedly died following a mining-site collapse around the boundary of Bassa, Jos South and Jos North local government areas. Four people died in another mining-site collapse in Dura, Jos South, in September 2025. In December 2025, 12 people were reportedly killed in an attack at Ratoso Fan in Barkin Ladi, while seven others were killed in a shooting incident at Kuru, Jos South, in January 2026. In February 2026, at least 37 people died at Kampanin Zurak in Wase Local Government Area following exposure to toxic gas at a mining site. Five people were killed at Gero Village, Gyel, in Jos South, on June 16, 2026, while three others were killed at Nyango-Gyere on June 30, with two others injured. On August 12, seven people died in a mining-pit collapse in Kassa, Barkin Ladi, while two others were killed in another incident in Gangare, Barkin Ladi, on September 23. The reported deaths amount to 90. Concerned by the situation, Governor Caleb Mutfwang, in February 2025, issued Executive Order 001 suspending mining activities across 17 local government areas. In May 2025, the state government said 159 operators had been cleared to operate under various categories, including six mining licences, 15 small-scale mining leases, 15 exploration licences, five artisanal and small-scale mining permits, one quarry lease and 118 tin sheds and buying centres. However, the remote and scattered nature of mining sites, coupled with reports of night operations, has continued to pose challenges to effective monitoring. KOGI: Battle for gold, others Kogi State Government has expressed concern over illegal mining, particularly in areas where mining activities have affected communities and the environment. In September 2026, Alake, while responding to protesting youths in the state, described illegal mining as a major concern. He said Mining Marshals had dislodged illegal miners operating in a licensed area in Yagba East Local Government Area. The minister said investigations indicated that some of the illegal miners were indigenes and alleged that some elders, traditional rulers and local government functionaries supported the activities. The Concerned Kogi Youths Against Environmental Degradation had protested against the impact of mining in areas including Ankpa and Omala, alleging that the activities had damaged roads, destroyed farmland and polluted water sources. Kogi is endowed with coal and other mineral resources, making regulation and monitoring of mining activities a continuing challenge. NASARAWA: Lithium frontier Nasarawa State has emerged as one of the country’s important lithium-mining areas, with activities particularly reported in Kokona, Wamba and Nasarawa Eggon local government areas. The state has attracted both local and foreign operators, leading to increased regulatory and security attention. In May 2026, 15 Chinese nationals and nine Nigerians were arraigned before the Federal High Court in Abuja over alleged illegal lithium mining in Kokona Local Government Area. Concerns have also been raised over the safety of workers and possible child labour at mining sites. In September, special monitoring and enforcement teams intensified checks on mining operations, particularly to ensure that operators remained within licensed coordinates. TARABA: Repeated suspensions Across the forests, rugged mountains and river basins of Taraba State, illegal mining has emerged as a major environmental and security concern. Taraba sits atop deposits of gold, blue sapphire, topaz, lead, zinc and lithium. Yet, over the years, these resources have increasingly attracted unauthorised mining activities. Unauthorised miners have moved into parts of the state, including forest reserves and rural settlements. The most intense activities have been reported around Mayokam and Gangtu in Bali, the Mambilla Plateau in Sardauna, Takum, Ardo-Kola and Gassol. Security profiling and intelligence reports indicate that some mining camps involve migrant labourers and undocumented foreigners from Cameroon. Security agencies have carried out raids in several areas, arresting hundreds of miners reportedly from Zamfara, Katsina and Bauchi states. The activities also involve networks of middlemen, mineral buyers, financiers and operators of heavy equipment. Governor Agbu Kefas has issued three Executive Orders suspending mining activities since 2023, including another suspension in June 2026. Illegal mining has been documented across Sardauna, Karim Lamido, Bali, Gashaka, Kurmi, Ussa and Yorro local government areas. A Premium Times investigation estimated that the state could lose more than N10 billion annually to illegal mining. On September 18, 2026, five alleged illegal miners died following a mining-pit collapse in Mayokam, Bali Local Government Area. A task force subsequently dispersed miners and seized equipment, with reports indicating that some of the miners were from Zamfara, Bauchi and Sokoto states, as well as Cameroon and Chad. EBONYI: Abandoned pits, deaths Ebonyi State is endowed with mineral resources including limestone, zinc, lead, chalcopyrite and oxide. While mining licences are issued by the Federal Government, the state government has environmental and community-level responsibilities, creating an additional layer of regulation and enforcement. The state has faced allegations of unlicensed mining operations, poor environmental practices and failure by some operators to carry out required environmental impact assessments. Mining activities and abandoned pits have been reported in areas including Abakaliki, Ikwo, Izzi, Ezza South, Ebonyi and Ishielu. The state government, in collaboration with the NSCDC, has announced measures against illegal mining and unauthorised mineral trading. Abandoned mining pits have remained a major concern in communities including Okposi Umuoghara, Enyigba, Ameka and Ishiagu. There have also been allegations of child labour and the involvement of pregnant women in mining activities. The state government inaugurated a Solid Minerals Task Force to seal illegal sites, confiscate equipment and stop night-time rock crushing and the movement of mineral-laden trucks. Licensed operators are expected to comply with the Mining Act, display appropriate signposts, pay required revenue, refrain from night operations, conduct environmental impact assessments and enter into Community Development Agreements where applicable. The Commissioner for Solid Minerals, Mt Magnus Nkah, during visits to mining communities in Ishielu and Ohaukwu, warned operators to comply with safety requirements. “The welfare of workers is equally important because these workers are our people. Many companies have not paid sufficient attention to their welfare,” he said. The government has also raised concerns about inadequate safety standards and delays in implementing community development agreements and other obligations, including scholarships. The ministry said it would issue compliance templates and deadlines, while the task force would monitor operations and work to eliminate revenue leakages. Night-time transportation of minerals has also been declared illegal in affected areas. The dangers posed by abandoned pits have already resulted in deaths. Community youth leader Ogochukwu Elem said one abandoned pit had remained open for about 10 years after an earlier incident. At Okposi Umuoghara, a truck driver and his assistant reportedly died after falling into a mining pit. A motorcycle operator later died after falling into the same pit when his brakes reportedly failed, while a cyclist also died in the area. The incidents accounted for at least five deaths. In Ezza North, three suspects were arrested by the NSCDC over alleged illegal mining, while the site was sealed. BAUCHI: Mining, insecurity concerns Illegal mining has become a security concern in parts of Bauchi State, particularly in Alkaleri and neighbouring border communities. In August 2026, Governor Bala Mohammed identified illegal mining in the area as a major contributor to insecurity and banditry and warned influential individuals allegedly involved in the activities that they could face prosecution. Illegal mining does not automatically cause banditry. However, the presence of valuable minerals and uncontrolled mining operations can create opportunities for armed groups and other criminal networks to exploit weak regulation and security gaps. KADUNA: Gold, tin, lithium Mining activities have been reported in Birnin Gwari, Sanga, Jema’a and Kubau local government areas of Kaduna State. The state has deposits of gold, tin, tantalum, lithium and gemstones. A 2024 study identified 103 mining sites across 36 communities in four local government areas, comprising 53 active and 50 abandoned sites. The study identified Jema’a and Birnin Gwari as major areas of activity, while Sanga and Kajuru also recorded mining operations. In Birnin Gwari, communities including Fara Ruwa, Bugai, Dagara, Awaro, Tashan Keji, Sabon Layi, Dawakin Basa, Kungi, Janruwa, Maganda, Tsohon Gwari, Randagi and Rema have reported mining activities involving gold, tin, tantalum and tourmaline. At a gold-mining site around Bugai, about 16 kilometres from Birnin Gwari, miners described the activity as an important source of livelihood, although many operators remain outside the formal licensing system. The Birnin Gwari Emirate Progressive Union, BEPU, has called for stronger security around mining communities. In Jema’a, the study identified 64 mining sites, accounting for more than 60 per cent of its sample. Communities mentioned include Godogodo, Gidan Waya, Antang, Nisama, Kanufi, Zankan-Nindem, Gwaska, Dangoma, Garti, Farin Hawa and Ambam. Minerals reported in the area include tantalite, tourmaline, tin, lithium, mica, zircon, sapphire and nickel. In May 2025, illegal tin-mining operations in Damau, Kubau Local Government Area, were shut down. The Kaduna State development plan has also identified indiscriminate mining, particularly in Birnin Gwari and Jema’a, as a cause of land degradation. KEBBI: Gold, informal operations In February 2026, Mining Marshals, supported by the Department of State Services, the Army and the Police, dislodged thousands of people from mining areas under the Presidential Artisanal Gold Mining Development Initiative, PAGMI, in Yauri Local Government Area. Gold is the dominant mineral in the affected areas. The government has sought to formalise artisanal mining through initiatives such as PAGMI, but informal operations have continued to pose challenges. Environmental concerns include land degradation and pollution of water sources. The continuing challenge is how to prevent operators displaced by enforcement operations from simply moving to other unregulated mining locations. ADAMAWA: Mining, security concerns Mining activities in Adamawa State have also attracted security concerns. The state has deposits of gold, limestone and gypsum, with mining activities reported in Song, Mubi, Maiha, Jada, Toungo and Michika. In June 2026, Governor Ahmadu Fintiri ordered an immediate ban on illegal mining in Lamurde following a preliminary report on a crisis in the area and directed security agencies to enforce the order. As in other states, mining does not automatically create every conflict, but uncontrolled mining can deepen tensions over land, access to resources and local revenue. BENUE: Displacement Mining activities have continued in parts of Benue State, particularly in Kwande and Logo local government areas. Communities affected include Mbagber, Tombo, Ukemberagya/Tswarev and Ayilamo. The activities have taken place alongside attacks and displacement in parts of the state. Federal lawmaker Terseer Ugbor has linked illegal mining to insecurity in the state, although such claims represent a political assessment and should not be taken as proof of a direct causal relationship. The Turan Development Association suspended mining activities in May, citing insecurity, environmental degradation and alleged exploitation. The state government has also cautioned traditional rulers against issuing mining permits without the necessary approvals. OSUN: Foreign illegal miners Illegal mining in Osun State is not only disrupting livelihoods, especially on ancient farmlands, including cocoa and kolanut plantations, but is also creating environmental hazards that constitute inherent dangers to the lives and property of residents and indigenes of affected communities. The menace mostly affects Osun-East Senatorial District, particularly Ifeland and Ijesaland, but the environmental impact extends to Osogbo, Asejire and the Osun River. There has been an influx of illegal miners from northern Nigeria, Niger Republic and Mali, with concerns over inadequate documentation and the security implications. In Ijesaland, affected communities include Ibodi, Ijanna Wasare, Itagunmodi, Ayegunle, Iwara, Igangan, Kajola, Iponda, Ikinyinwa and Ilase. Ile-Ife, Ifetedo and Ifewara have also recorded mining activities. Farmlands have reportedly been destroyed, forcing some farmers and farm owners to abandon their lands, while residents living close to mining sites have also abandoned their houses. There have been allegations that some influential indigenes backed illegal mining activities for pecuniary gains, while officials allegedly shielded miners through a ticketing system operated by third parties. During a visit by Sunday Vanguard to Ibodi alongside officials of the Federal Ministry of Solid Minerals Development and four local government chairmen, security personnel were allegedly seen providing cover for miners and preventing enforcement officers from carrying out arrests, citing legal tickets issued to the operators. The situation reportedly led to a standoff, with Sanya Omirin intervening. Military and police personnel were also reported to have raised weapons against one another during the confrontation. At Ijanna Wasare, NSCDC personnel were allegedly accused of alerting miners and helping some of them escape, thereby preventing arrests. The Osun-Osogbo River serves more than 20 communities, and pollution allegedly linked to gold mining has raised concerns about its use and consumption. Concerned by the development, Urban Alert called for urgent intervention by federal government, Osun State government and international partners. The organisation said the river stretches about 213 kilometres from Ekiti through Osun, Oyo and Ogun to Lagos, with five dams and about two million people depending on it. Urban Alert said testing had detected substances including cyanide, mercury and lead, raising concerns about possible health risks. Chairman of Ilesa West Local Government Area, Lanre Balogun, said many mining sites had no records with the Federal Ministry of Solid Minerals Development and were operating without licences. He said the local government had sought information from the Osun Mining Office but had not received a satisfactory response, adding that unknown individuals were collecting revenue through ticketing. “We discovered that many of these mining sites have no records whatsoever with the Federal Ministry of Solid Minerals Development. They are unregistered, unlicensed and largely untraceable. Rather than enforcement, what we observed was the unlawful collection of revenue by unknown artisanal miners at the expense of the safety of our communities,” Balogun said. OYO: Gold, gemstones, marble Illegal mining activities have been reported across Oke-Ogun, Iwajowa, Iseyin, Itesiwaju, Atisbo, Kajola and Irepo, as well as parts of Ido, Egbeda and Lagelu local government areas. The Lagos-Ibadan quarry axis has also recorded mining activities, while Itasa in Iwajowa has attracted attention over mineral exploitation. Minerals found across the state include gold, tantalite, tourmaline, gemstones, aquamarine, sapphire, talc, marble, kaolin, quartz, cassiterite, columbite, bismuth, granite, feldspar and clay. Parts of Ibarapa are known for tantalite, aquamarine, tourmaline and sapphire, while Irepo has marble and tantalite deposits. Igbeti in Olorunsogo is also known for marble and dolomite. There have been allegations of the involvement of some traditional rulers in mining activities. In January 2026, the state government suspended the Sobaloju of Ofiki, Atisbo Local Government Area, over allegations that he issued unauthorised consent letters to mining companies and permitted mining activities in a government reserve. The case has also highlighted tensions between federal control of mining titles and state and community interests in environmental protection and local development. OGUN: Lithium, gold, quarrying Illegal mining has been reported around Ogere in Ikenne, Ode-Remo in Remo North, the Omi-Ogunmakin-Odede axis and other border communities. Minerals found in the state include lithium, mica, gold, tantalite, granite, feldspar, kaolin, silica sand and clay. The expansion of mining activities has raised concerns over environmental degradation, land use and the regulation of operators working outside the formal licensing framework. EDO: Gold, lithium, other minerals Mining activities have been reported across Edo North, including Okpella, Ososo and the Egbetua forest axis in Etsako East and Akoko-Edo local government areas. Other locations include Erhua near Ehor and Iruekpen. Minerals associated with the state include gold, lithium, iron ore, titanium, granite, marble, limestone, kaolin, feldspar and silica. The spread of unauthorised mining has raised concerns over forest degradation, land use and the environmental impact of mining operations. KWARA: Gold, lithium Illegal mining activities have been reported in Kaiama and Bani, with gold and lithium among the minerals attracting operators. Kwara is also endowed with tantalite, cassiterite, columbite, tourmaline, aquamarine, sapphire, emerald, amethyst, beryl, marble, dolomite, kaolin, quartz, feldspar, granite and talc. The expansion of unauthorised mining has raised concerns over environmental degradation, revenue leakage and the difficulty of monitoring remote mining locations. National security Security expert, Dr Bamaiyi Altine, said the government should treat illegal mining as a national security issue, arguing that proceeds from the activities could provide resources for armed groups. “Government should treat this as a national security issue. These people are unregulated and mean. They are lawless in areas they operate. I don’t think the Mining Marshals alone can checkmate their activities. As long as these activities continue unchecked, banditry will remain active,” Altine said. Another security expert, Mr Okwuonye Eziashi, called for urgent government action, warning against allowing illegal mining to develop into another major security crisis. He said: “Government needs to act fast. We should not wait until illegal mining becomes another full-blown security crisis before we respond. What we are seeing in some parts of the country should concern everybody because wherever you have valuable minerals being exploited outside the law, you can also have criminal elements taking advantage of the situation. “We have the experience of the Democratic Republic of Congo to learn from. The battle for control of mineral resources has been intertwined with armed conflict in eastern Congo for decades. Different armed groups have benefited from the illicit exploitation and trade in minerals. We cannot afford to allow a similar pattern to develop here. “The lesson for Nigeria is clear: we must secure our mining communities, regulate the sector properly and ensure that proceeds from our mineral resources do not end up financing banditry, terrorism or other criminal activities. The earlier government moves decisively, the easier it will be to prevent illegal mining from becoming a major driver of insecurity.” ILLEGAL MINING: Children face brain, lung, reproductive damage—Experts By Chioma Obinna For children growing up around mining sites, danger can be difficult to see. It may be in the fine dust hanging in the air, the water flowing from a contaminated stream, the soil beneath bare feet, or the food produced near where minerals are extracted. It may also be in the long hours spent at a mining site instead of sitting in a classroom. The issue was recently brought into focus when young children in Niger and Plateau states were found involved in illegal mining, once again drawing attention to the growing vulnerability of minors around mining communities. But beyond child labour and lost schooling lies another danger that may be less visible and far more enduring. What exposure to the mining environment can do to a developing child. Experts in pharmacology, toxicology, public health and reproductive health said that exposure to mining activities can cause neurological, respiratory and developmental damage. At the same time, heavy metals and other contaminants may threaten reproductive health and contaminate entire communities. For Prof. Omoniyi Yemitan, Professor of Pharmacology and Toxicology at the Lagos State University College of Medicine, Ikeja, in an interview with Sunday Vanguard, the problem is not mining itself but what happens when basic safety precautions are ignored, particularly in artisanal mining. “Mining is a problem all over the world. It’s not only in Nigeria, but it is more problematic when necessary precautions are not carried out for miners,” he said. In a properly regulated environment, miners are expected to use protective equipment, including helmets, gas or nose masks, coveralls and safety boots. But many artisanal miners lack the knowledge, resources or discipline to adhere to such safety measures. That becomes particularly troubling when children live, play or work around the same sites. Yemitan said children could inhale heavy metals associated with minerals being extracted, as well as other metals present in surrounding soil and rock. Gold, tin and, increasingly, lithium have attracted attention in Nigeria, but the minerals being extracted may occur alongside other substances capable of causing harm. “They always have some lead in their environment, mercury in the environment and all that. And all those, when they are inhaled, they have health implications, especially in children,” he said. Problem Mining environments can contain large quantities of dust carrying particles from soil, rock and chemicals present at mining sites. Prolonged inhalation can damage the respiratory system. For Yemitan, however, one of the most worrying consequences for children is neurological damage. “Toxic metal poisoning can cause brain damage,” he said, adding that prolonged exposure could interfere with cognitive development. The concern is not necessarily about an immediate and visible injury. A child may continue to attend school, play and appear healthy while toxic exposure gradually affects development. The professor said children exposed to mining could eventually have lower IQ levels than children who were not exposed, indicating that parts of the developing brain could be affected by toxic substances. But the danger does not stop with the brain. Yemitan identified the lungs as another major organ at risk, stressing that children could be particularly vulnerable because their respiratory systems were still developing. One of the conditions associated with prolonged exposure to dust from mining is silicosis, a lung disease caused by inhalation of respirable crystalline silica. “When scarring occurs, the functions of the lungs will be reduced,” he said. The consequences can spread throughout the body because inadequate oxygen supply affects vital organs, including the brain. “If enough oxygen is not getting to the brain, especially in children, then all the health issues which I mentioned originally about brain damage and low IQ will generally occur,” he said. Chronic cough, asthma and hypoxia, a condition in which the body does not receive sufficient oxygen, are also among the possible consequences of prolonged exposure, he added. Yet toxic exposure is only one layer of the danger. Mining site “The earth can at any time collapse on anybody, but more particularly children that don’t have enough guard for themselves,” Yemitan said. Nigeria has already witnessed the devastating consequences of unsafe mining, particularly in Zamfara State, where lead poisoning linked to artisanal gold mining has affected communities, including children. Yemitan recalled the health crises associated with mining in Zamfara and said other parts of the country had also experienced mining-related incidents. For children, he stressed, vulnerability is heightened by their stage of physical development. “Children are particularly more vulnerable when it comes to mining sites because their guard is, of course, reduced. Their bodies are still developing, so more prone to some of these health effects,” he said. But the hidden toll of mining does not necessarily stop at the edge of a mining site. Once toxic substances enter the environment, they can travel through water, soil, air and food. For Dr Casmier Ifeanyi, public health and medical research scientist and National President of the Association of Medical Laboratory Scientists of Nigeria, the consequences of poorly regulated mining are “very far-reaching” and potentially devastating. He said: “The implications of mining in any area, particularly the health-related implications, are very far-reaching. They are very devastating, and sometimes they lead up to lifelong debilitation. Nigeria’s experience with lead poisoning in Zamfara is a clear example of the consequences of illegal, unregulated and unsafe mining. “So the issue and the risks associated with mining for any community are well-documented.’’ According to him, mining exposes people to both physical hazards and toxicological risks. Children living near mining areas, as well as those directly involved in mining, could be exposed to heavy metals and chemicals through air, water, soil and other environmental pathways. He identified lead and mercury among substances of particular concern. Lead poisoning associated with artisanal gold mining, he said, could cause kidney damage and other serious health consequences, while mercury exposure could cause neurological damage. “Children who are exposed to mining may end up with brain damage, and would, of course, have developmental issues. This is well established,” he said. But perhaps one of the most troubling aspects of environmental contamination is that people may not know they are being exposed. Mining operations can pollute surface water and groundwater when minerals and mining waste are washed into water bodies. People may then be exposed through drinking water, farming and livestock. “The air in that environment again becomes very much polluted. If you aggregate it, people absorb this, the soil absorbs it, it ends up in the food we eat,” he said. The contamination can move far beyond the immediate mining community. “If you consume livestock produced in that area, the food you have grown in those areas that end up in Lagos and Abuja, and any other part of the world for that matter, would have absorbed these heavy metals,” he said. The concern is particularly significant in communities where people depend on groundwater, including boreholes, for domestic use. Ifeanyi said mining activities could contaminate water bodies used for farming, livestock production and domestic purposes. “People dig up anything, and they go to the freshwater body where people fetch for farming, where they fetch for livestock production, where they fetch for domestic use, and they go there to wash them. And as they wash, they are contaminating the water bodies. They are contaminating groundwater bodies,” he said. The implication is that a mining operation can affect people who have never entered a mining pit. Childhood There is another cost that cannot be measured through laboratory tests. Children drawn into mining can lose something that is difficult to recover later — their education and childhood. Ifeanyi said mining often involves hard labour and child labour, depriving children of education while exposing them to exploitation. Some children, he noted, are introduced to mining because they can earn small amounts of money from the activity. “That child will tell you, education is a scam. I am already making money,” he said. What appears to be an immediate opportunity to earn money can become a cycle of poverty in which children abandon school, become trapped in hazardous work and grow up with fewer opportunities to escape poverty. “It is exploitative. It’s exploitative, taking undue advantage of them,” he said. The consequences, however, may extend beyond childhood. Ifeanyi said some toxic metals associated with mining could affect reproductive health, creating risks that could extend beyond the individual who was exposed. He also raised concerns about sexual exploitation and early pregnancies around mining communities, saying children and young people in such environments could face multiple forms of vulnerability. “Exposing children to mining affects not only their health; it has psychological and social effects, it affects reproductive health, it has a transgenerational impact, and the communities where this happens are also not spared at all,” he said. That possibility introduces another dimension to the mining problem: the health of generations yet unborn. Generations For Prof. Oladapo Ashiru, renowned Nigerian professor of anatomy, reproductive endocrinologist and pioneer of In Vitro Fertilisation in West Africa, the reproductive-health consequences of mining exposure deserve particular attention. Ashiru warned that children exposed to toxic substances could face risks that affect their future ability to have healthy children. According to him, the mining environment creates a combination of physical hazards, toxic exposure and developmental vulnerability. Toxic substances such as lead and mercury can cross the placental barrier, potentially exposing unborn children and increasing the risk of developmental problems, impaired cognition, low birth weight and premature birth. He said exposure could also affect reproductive health before conception. “For women, hazardous exposure can contribute to reduced fertility, menstrual disorders and premature menopause, while in men it can affect hormone production, sperm count and sperm movement,” Ashiru said. “The reproductive implications are therefore not limited to children who are currently working in mining. Exposure among adults of reproductive age can potentially affect pregnancies and future generations.” For children actually working at mining sites, the risks begin much earlier. They may be injured in tunnel collapses, while handling explosives or using unsuitable tools. Carrying heavy loads can cause musculoskeletal injuries and deformities, particularly in growing bodies. The respiratory system is another major target. “Children who inhale rock dust over extended periods can develop serious respiratory disease, including silicosis. Exposure to mercury during gold extraction can damage the nervous system and result in symptoms such as tremors, mood changes and cognitive impairment, while lead exposure can interfere with normal neurodevelopment,” Ashiru said. The absence of protective equipment, he added, makes matters worse. “Children may inhale toxic substances or absorb them through their skin during mining activities, including when mercury amalgam is handled or burned.” Their developing organs, Ashiru said, make them particularly susceptible to the effects of toxic chemicals. But the health burden extends beyond poisoning, respiratory disease and physical injuries. Mining settlements can also face poor sanitation and inadequate access to healthcare, creating conditions that facilitate the spread of infectious diseases and making treatment more difficult for people already suffering from chronic exposure. “Children in mining communities may have limited access to medical facilities because of distance, cost and the economic circumstances of their families,” he said. That can create a vicious cycle: exposure causes illness; illness imposes medical and economic costs; poverty pushes families towards mining; and children are again exposed to hazardous conditions. Beyond the mining pit The picture that emerges is therefore much larger than whether an individual miner wears a helmet or safety boot. At stake is the health of entire communities and the long-term development of children growing up around mining operations. A contaminated stream does not remain within the boundaries of a mining site. Polluted water can affect households, livestock and farms. Dust can travel through communities. Toxic substances can enter food chains. And children, because their brains, lungs, immune systems and other organs are still developing, can bear a disproportionate share of the consequences. For Ifeanyi, Nigeria does not lack laws and policies to regulate the sector but suffers from weak implementation and enforcement. “We are not in short supply of laws. We are not in short supply of legislation,” he said. He called for greater investment in industrial-scale mining and a system capable of bringing artisanal miners into regulated structures where safety and environmental standards can be enforced. He also questioned the effectiveness of current oversight and called for comprehensive information on mining sites across the country. “What is difficult about that? The ministry should have data, a geopolitical survey of all points where people mine,” he said. According to him, Nigeria needs a comprehensive monitoring system capable of identifying legal and illegal mining operations and allowing authorities to intervene before environmental and health damage becomes widespread. “The ministry should have a dashboard where, at any time you know all the mining sites, whether it is illicit, artisanal, or large-scale, on a dashboard,” he said. Such a system, he argued, would make it easier to monitor mining operations, enforce environmental standards and clamp down on illegal activities. But regulation alone may not be enough. Protecting children requires education, healthcare, alternative livelihoods and strict protection from hazardous labour. Environmental monitoring must also extend beyond the mining site to water sources, farmland, food and surrounding settlements. Price Nigeria’s mineral wealth offers economic opportunities, but the experts’ warnings point to another side of the equation: the health cost of extracting that wealth when safety and environmental standards are ignored. The immediate image of mining may be men and women digging into the earth in search of valuable minerals. The less visible picture is different. It is dust entering a child’s lungs. Heavy metals affecting a developing brain. Contaminated water entering a household. Toxic substances moving from soil to crops, livestock and food. A child leaving school to work. And exposure potentially affecting reproductive health years after the mining activity has ended. For Yemitan, the basic message is clear: children should not be exposed to mining environments without protection, and mining operations must be subjected to safety standards that protect both workers and surrounding communities. For Ifeanyi, the challenge involves not only enforcement but also education, healthcare, alternative livelihoods and protection of children from exploitation. For Ashiru, the reproductive consequences add another dimension to the problem, raising questions about how today’s exposure could affect tomorrow’s parents and children. The experts maintained that mining is not merely an economic activity but a public health issue with consequences that can stretch across a lifetime and, in some cases, across generations. They argued that as Nigeria seeks to expand its solid minerals sector and attract greater investment into mining, economic development cannot be separated from public health. The post Mad rush into deadly pits for gold: 374 illegal mining sites in 17 states uncovered appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Missiles fired at Riyadh, intercepted by coalition
items.description: RIYADH: The Saudi-led coalition battling Yemen’s Houthis said on Saturday it had intercepted drones and ballistic missiles, as the group launched fresh attacks, including on Riyadh, despite international condemnation. A spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition said on Saturday its air defences “intercepted and destro­yed two drones launched by the Houthis towards the Riyadh area”. Saudi air defences also intercepted and destroyed two Houthi-launched ballistic missiles targeting Khamis Mushait, a city in the country’s southwest that is home to an air base, the spokesman said. Hezam Al-Assad, a member of the Houthi Political Bureau, said on Saturday that “Despite the operation’s strength, scope, and impact, our armed forces view it as merely a small-scale rehearsal for a full-scale escalation.” Meanwhile, Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, secretary general of the Gulf Cooperation Council, denounced the Houthi attacks. “This dangerous escalation constitutes a flagrant violation of the Kingdom’s sovereignty and poses a direct threat to the security and safety of civilians and the stability of the region,” he said in a statement. Published in Dawn, September 27th, 2026

items.title: IHC voids law allowing agencies to curb travel
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The Islamabad High Court (IHC) has declared unconstitutional a provision of the Passport Rules, 2021, that allowed the placement of a citizen’s name on the Passport Control List (PCL) on the recommendation of government agencies or departments without identifying a competent authority or providing legal safeguards. Justice Raja Inaam Ameen Minhas, in a detailed judgement, declared the second limb of Rule 22(2)(b) ultra vires the Passports Act, 1974, and Articles 4, 9, 10A and 15 of the Constitution, holding that it was of no legal effect. The judgement was issued on a petition filed by Moinuddin, who was offloaded at Islamabad International Airport on Dec 18, 2025, while travelling to Saudi Arabia for Umrah. He possessed a valid Pakistani passport, a valid Saudi visa and a confirmed air ticket, but no reason was communicated to him for stopping him from travelling. The court noted that his passport had never been impounded, confiscated, cancelled or inactivated, nor had its issuance or renewal been refused. The dispute, therefore, centred on the question whether the agency had the authority to restrain a citizen from travelling on a valid passport. According to the judgement, his name was placed on the PCL on Dec 24, 2024, on the recommendation of NCB-INTERPOL, forwarded by the FIA’s Assistant Director (Immigration Wing). The action followed his deportation from the UK after his conviction for causing death by dangerous driving while under the influence of alcohol. He had served a three-year sentence. The court noted that he had completed his sentence and been deported, while no criminal case, inquiry or investigation was pending against him in Pakistan. He was neither a proclaimed offender nor the subject of an extradition request. The IHC rejected the justification provided by the passport authorities to retain his name on the PCL that his conduct had adversely affected Pakistan’s reputation and that the placement was intended to create deterrence. The court observed that these grounds were not contained in the Passports Act or the Passport Rules. Rule 21 dealt with refusal of a passport and did not authorise restraint of a citizen who already possessed a valid passport, the judgement stated. “The refusal of a passport and the prohibition of travel are two separate exercises of power,” Justice Minhas observed, declaring that the function of the relevant division and directorate general to “prepare and maintain” the PCL was administrative and did not itself confer jurisdiction to decide whose name could be placed on the list. The court pointed out that Rule 22(2) referred to individuals whose passport facilities had been refused. Moinuddin had never been refused a passport. It also noted that Rule 22(2)(a) specifically identified the additional secretary of the relevant division as the authority competent to place and remove names in Category A, whereas clause (b) identified no such authority. The IHC held that neither the directorate general of FIA nor NCB-INTERPOL possessed the authority to place the petitioner’s name on the PCL in the circumstances of the case. It observed that the impugned order merely stated that it had been issued with the approval of the “competent authority” without identifying that authority, the legal provision invoked or the material on which the decision was based. The court found that the impugned provision provided no competent authority, objective criteria, notice, hearing, reasons or communication of the decision, meaning that a citizen could learn of the restriction only after being stopped at the immigration counter. The judgement declared the second limb of Rule 22(2)(b) — allowing PCL placement on the recommendations of government agencies or departments — beyond Sections 8 and 13 of the Passports Act and inconsistent with the Constitution. About the reasons of “international reputation” and “deterrence”, the court held that since the petitioner had completed his sentence and no proceedings were pending against him, the restraint had no “live and proximate nexus with a present necessity”. “Gravity does not supply jurisdiction,” it said. Expressing displeasure over the authorities’ failure to comply with an earlier order, the IHC directed them to decide the petitioner’s application within one week through a speaking and well-reasoned order. The court consequently set aside the Jan 26, 2026, order of the agency and declared the petitioner’s placement on the PCL on Dec 24, 2024, without lawful authority and of no legal effect. It directed the authorities to remove his name from the PCL within 15 days of receiving a certified copy of the judgement and not to interfere with his lawful foreign travel on the basis of the impugned placement. The court clarified that the competent authority could still take action warranted by law after following the prescribed procedure. Copies of the judgement were sent to the Interior Secretary, Immigration and Passports DG and FIA DG for compliance. Published in Dawn, September 27th, 2026
